--- Makefile ---
PROJECT_HOME := .
VULTRON_DIR := $(PROJECT_HOME)/vultron
TEST_DIR := $(PROJECT_HOME)/test

# Load environment variables from .env file if it exists
ifneq (,$(wildcard .env))
  include .env
  export
endif

PROJECT_NAME ?= vultron

# Display help information about available targets
.PHONY: help
help:  ## Show this help message
	@grep -E '^[a-zA-Z_-]+:.*?## .*$$' $(filter-out .env,$(MAKEFILE_LIST)) | sort | awk 'BEGIN {FS = ":.*?## "}; {printf "  %-20s %s\n", $$1, $$2}'

# set up dev environment
.PHONY: setup_dev
setup_dev:  ## Set up development environment
	uv sync --dev

# upgrade dev dependencies
.PHONY: upgrade_dev
upgrade_dev:  ## Upgrade dev dependencies
	uv sync --upgrade --dev

# upgrade dependencies
.PHONY: upgrade_deps
upgrade_deps:  ## Upgrade all dependencies
	uv sync --upgrade

# run tests locally
.PHONY: test
test:  ## Run tests locally
	uv run pytest test

# black code formatting
.PHONY: black
black:  ## Format code with black
	uv run black .

# markdownlint-cli2 code formatting
.PHONY: mdlint
mdlint:  ## Lint markdown files
	./mdlint.sh

# flake8
.PHONY: flake8
flake8:  ## Check code with flake8
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.flake8 to configure flake8 options
	uv run flake8 ${VULTRON_DIR} ${TEST_DIR}

# flake8 code linting
.PHONY: flake8-lint
flake8-lint:  ## Lint code with flake8
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.flake8 to configure flake8 options
	uv run flake8 --exit-zero ${VULTRON_DIR} ${TEST_DIR}

# mypy type checking
.PHONY: mypy
mypy:  ## Run mypy for type checking
	# edit $(PROJECT_HOME)/.mypy.ini to configure mypy options
	uv run mypy

# pyright static type checking
.PHONY: pyright
pyright:  ## Run pyright for static type checking
	uv run pyright

# run all linters
.PHONY: lint
lint: black mdlint flake8-lint mypy ## Run all linters (black, markdownlint)

# serve docs locally
.PHONY: docs
docs:  ## Serve documentation locally
	uv run mkdocs serve

We're using the expanded concept of an Any Decision Record (ADR) to capture any decision that is important to the project, not just architectural decisions. We use Markdown Any Decision Records (MADR) to document our architectural decisions.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#when-to-write-an-adr","title":"When to write an ADR","text":"<p>The primary signal for an ADR is evaluated alternatives: if you considered more than one option and rejected at least one, document the decision. The record preserves context for future maintainers who might otherwise re-open a settled question.</p> <p>Concretely, write an ADR when:</p> <ul> <li>You adopted a structural or architectural approach over one or more   alternatives (e.g., hexagonal architecture over layered, SQLModel over   TinyDB).</li> <li>You made a one-time process or tooling decision with lasting project-wide   impact (e.g., CalVer over SemVer, pinning CI action SHAs).</li> <li>A decision will be hard or costly to reverse, so the rationale should be   preserved explicitly.</li> </ul> <p>ADR vs. spec: an ADR records why a choice was made; a spec entry records what the system must do going forward. When a significant decision also generates recurring testable requirements, create both \u2014 see <code>notes/specs-vs-adrs.md</code> for the full delineation guidelines and worked examples.</p> <p>You do not need an ADR for:</p> <ul> <li>Uncontested conventions with no real alternatives (write a spec entry   instead).</li> <li>Small tactical choices where the rationale is obvious from the code.</li> </ul> <p>If you're unsure, err on the side of writing one \u2014 a brief ADR is better than losing context.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#how-to-write-an-adr","title":"How to write an ADR","text":"<p>For new ADRs, please use adr-template.md as basis. ActivityStreams 2.0 (AS2) structural types leaked into domain logic; semantic extraction was scattered across multiple files; handler functions instantiated the persistence layer directly; and the root <code>vultron/</code> package mixed domain enums with wire-format enums. requires every object to have an <code>id</code> field. The <code>generate_new_id()</code> utility in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/utils.py</code> currently returns a bare UUID-4 string (e.g., <code>2196cbb2-fb6f-407c-b473-1ed8ae806578</code>) as the default <code>as_id</code> for new objects. The AS2 specification and the Vultron object-IDs spec (<code>specs/object-ids.yaml</code> OID-01-001) require that <code>id</code> values be full URI identifiers. Bare UUIDs are not valid AS2 identifiers and will cause interoperability problems once federation is implemented.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>AS2 compliance: ActivityStreams 2.0 requires <code>id</code> to be an absolute   IRI. Bare UUIDs are not IRIs.</li> <li>Federation readiness: Federated delivery requires globally unique,   resolvable identifiers. Bare UUIDs cannot be resolved across systems.</li> <li>Blackboard key safety: py_trees blackboard keys derived from full-URI   IDs must not use the raw URI (which contains slashes). Using the last path   segment or UUID suffix as the key avoids hierarchical key-parsing issues   (OID-03-001).</li> <li>DataLayer compatibility: The DataLayer uses <code>as_id</code> as the primary   lookup key. Changing the default ID format is a forward-looking migration;   any existing bare-UUID records are a prototype artifact.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li><code>urn:uuid:</code> prefix \u2014 <code>urn:uuid:{uuid4}</code> (e.g., PR #577 added an <code>_STUB_OBJECT_MODEL_MAP</code> workaround in <code>outbox_handler.py</code> that covers only <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> and requires per-type manual registration.</p> <p>Wire-format concerns also leak into the domain: AS2 freely models a nested object as an inline object, a bare ID string, or a <code>Link</code> reference, which forces core fields into <code>Object | str | Link | None</code> unions. has not been carved deeply enough to prevent agents and code from conflating them.</p> <p>Evidence: A two-actor demo run (case <code>urn:uuid:0f69d289-734f-47af-afd2-37091895371a</code>, 2026-06-12) actual protocol-significant activities (<code>validate_report</code>, <code>accept_report</code>, <code>propose_embargo</code>, <code>accept_embargo</code>, <code>notify_*</code>, separating the two logs so future agents and contributors stop using <code>record_event()</code> as a generic \"log this thing\" Statement","text":"<p>The two-actor demo CI invariant test (<code>test_invariant_5_expected_event_types_present</code>) failed after PR #1024 introduced the CASE_MANAGER role gate on <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. Investigation (issue #1026) revealed that most vendor-side trigger and received-side use cases never send an activity to the CaseActor's inbox. Consequently the CaseActor's canonical ledger was missing entries for <code>validate_report</code>, <code>ack_report</code>, <code>add_note_to_case</code>, <code>invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, <code>accept_invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, and <code>close_case</code>.</p> <p>Deeper inspection found that some received-side use cases (<code>note.py</code>, <code>embargo.py</code>) worked around this by resolving the CaseActor's ID from the DataLayer and then executing <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> with <code>actor_id=case_actor_id</code> \u2014 even when the use case was running inside the vendor actor's inbox, not the CaseActor's. This violates the identity contract documented in ADR-0018 and the identity-spoofing pitfall in <code>AGENTS.md</code>: a received-side use case MUST NOT execute a BT with an <code>actor_id</code> different from the actor whose DataLayer is active. The guarded commit BT emits <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> activities as if authored by the CaseActor while running in the wrong actor's outbox context, which is either silently dropped or produces hash-chain divergence.</p> <p>The project has stated this rule in scattered form across <code>AGENTS.md</code>, <code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code>, and <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code>, but the explicit, ADR-level statement of the only correct end-to-end path has been missing. As a result, agents and contributors keep re-discovering the shortcut (resolve CaseActor ID, run BT) and believing it is a valid \"delegation\" pattern.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> establishes that all post-creation   participant messages route through the Case Actor exclusively.</li> <li>ADR-0018 established a single-writer canonical ledger authored by the   CaseActor. Every protocol-significant trigger tree emits an outbound activity addressed to <code>case_manager_id</code>. ASGI delivers it to the CaseActor's inbox. The CaseActor's received use case checks <code>receiving_actor_id == case_actor_id</code> before executing the guarded commit \u2014 and only executes it when the check passes. Non-CaseActor received use cases do nothing at the commit step; they rely on the fact that the CaseActor's inbox will separately receive the same activity.</p> <p>Option B \u2014 \"Delegation\" via foreign actor_id resolution. This is the pattern already implemented correctly in <code>status.py</code>'s <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code> and MUST be applied to every received-side use case that participates in ledger entry authorship.</p> <p>Why <code>announce_case_ledger_entry</code> is excluded from <code>EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES</code>: <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> is the replication envelope: the mechanism by which the CaseActor broadcasts its canonical entries to participants. It cannot appear as the <code>payloadSnapshot</code> of a canonical entry because the snapshot is the protocol activity that triggered the entry, not the replication envelope that delivers it. Including it in <code>EXPECTED_EVENT_TYPES</code> for the case-actor log creates a circular requirement that can never be satisfied without corrupting the ledger.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good, because the delivery mechanism (ASGI self-delivery) is the same   trusted path already proven to work for case creation and status events. The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. OX-08-004 narrows its WARNING scope to exclude this purposeful self-copy pattern (the only valid use of <code>cc:</code> in the protocol).</p> <p>The working precedent for this pattern is <code>offer_case_manager_role</code>: its <code>ResolveCaseManagerOfferContextNode</code> sets <code>blackboard.offer_case_manager_to = [case_actor_id]</code> and the Offer is addressed to the CaseActor's own ID in <code>to:</code> (a special case where the CaseActor is genuinely the primary recipient). The <code>invite_actor_to_case</code> fix follows the same principle but uses <code>cc:</code> because the invitee is the primary recipient.</p> <p>Distinguishing self-delivery from external delivery in received-side use cases: The CaseActor's received-side <code>InviteActorToCaseReceivedUseCase</code> does not need to special-case \"did I send this myself?\" \u2014 the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code>'s <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> role gate is the only pre-flight guard needed. Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing","text":""},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. Investigation found <code>receiving_actor_id</code> is already resolved before dispatch (<code>FastAPIDispatchAdapter.dispatch()</code>, which sets it from the canonical actor ID resolved off the inbox URL path) and is already present on every received-side event by the time <code>execute()</code> runs. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code>   BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree. After FUZZ-01 through FUZZ-07 (#860\u2013#866), each call-out point has a probabilistic fuzzer node as its stand-in. The fuzzer is not a permanent implementation: it is an adapter that will be replaced over time by real data lookups, policy evaluations, or coordination agents.</p> <p>Before those replacements can happen, the call-out points must be expressed as proper injection seams: the BT tree must be built so that the fuzzer is the default backend, not the only option. Without an abstraction layer, swapping any call-out point requires finding and editing the concrete node class instead of injecting a different factory \u2014 and with roughly 93 call-out point nodes across all domains, the maintenance burden is unacceptable.</p> <p>The design question is: What mechanism makes each call-out point backend swappable while remaining consistent with the existing py_trees Behaviour pattern, factory-function conventions, and blackboard contract model?</p> <p>Design status \u2014 formed in sand, not concrete: This ADR captures the forward-looking intent after one planning session. The design will be exercised in #1151 (one exemplar per agent shape) and is expected to converge after two or three concrete implementations across different domain areas. Implementers working on the shape-based follow-on issues (FUZZ-08d through FUZZ-08g) SHOULD refine this ADR if the pattern proves incorrect or incomplete. The ADR status will advance from <code>proposed</code> to <code>accepted</code> once the exemplars validate the approach.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Must be consistent with the existing BT factory-function pattern   (tree composition functions, not ad-hoc node instantiation)</li> <li>Must allow individual call-out points to be swapped without changing the   calling tree structure (incremental replacement)</li> <li>Must maintain the same blackboard contract whether the backend is a fuzzer   or a real implementation \u2014 downstream nodes must be unaffected by the swap</li> <li>Must keep simulation artifacts (<code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>) out of   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> (BT-16-001)</li> <li>Must be compatible with the four agent shapes from ADR-0024 (Sentinel,   Evaluator, Retriever, Composer), each of which has different input/output   semantics</li> <li>Must support partial replacement: a scenario can use real implementations   for some call-out points and fuzzer backends for others in the same run</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>No abstraction \u2014 leave fuzzer nodes as concrete hardcoded classes; Types","text":""},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>Core domain helpers throughout <code>vultron/core/</code> are peppered with <code>if x is None: return None</code> chains. These silent failures propagate far from their source \u2014 the error surfaces at the point of use rather than the point of origin, making debugging difficult and creating a class of bug where program state is quietly corrupted or silently skipped.</p> <p>The root cause is structural: loose wire-layer types (where <code>Optional</code> fields are correct \u2014 AS2 permits many fields to be absent) leak directly into core logic without being promoted to tighter representations. Core functions then defensively guard every field they actually require.</p> <p>A secondary symptom is collection-typed fields and parameters that default to <code>None</code> instead of an empty collection, forcing every call-site to write <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate before iteration.</p> <p>The DataLayer already established the right precedent: <code>dl.read()</code> raises <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> rather than returning <code>None</code>. This ADR generalises that precedent to all core domain helpers and domain model fields.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Silent <code>None</code> propagation causes failures far from the error source.</li> <li>Core functions should express their contracts in their type signatures.</li> <li>The type system should make illegal states unrepresentable within core logic.</li> <li>Idiomatic Python prefers <code>raise</code> over sentinel return values (EAFP culture).</li> <li><code>dl.read()</code> raising <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> is an existing, working precedent   to generalise from.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>Return <code>None</code> and guard at every call-site \u2014 current pattern.</li> <li><code>Result</code>/<code>Option</code> monadic types (e.g. the <code>returns</code> library).</li> <li>One rich domain class with Optional fields and <code>None</code> guards in core.</li> <li>Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types (chosen).</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Validate at the edge, promote to strict core types, because it is idiomatic Python, fail-fast, provides a stack trace pointing to the origin of the error, and allows the type checker to verify guarantees.</p> <p>The pattern in three steps:</p> <ol> <li>Edge objects may be loose. Wire-layer and adapter Pydantic models may    have <code>Optional</code> fields where the protocol or external source permits absence.</li> <li>Promote at the boundary. At the boundary (extractor, rehydration layer,    use-case entry point), required fields are validated. If absent, a    descriptive exception is raised immediately \u2014 not propagated as <code>None</code>.</li> <li>Core receives strict types. What crosses into core logic is a type that    makes the required fields non-optional. Core functions declare these tighter    types in their signatures; the type system enforces the contract.</li> </ol> <p>The Vultron analogy for the blog post's drone pattern: <code>VultronActivity</code> (wire, loose) \u2192 validated at extractor/rehydration \u2192 <code>FooReceivedEvent</code> or use-case request type (core, tight). The role-specific <code>CaseParticipant</code> subclasses (<code>VendorParticipant</code>, etc.) are a partial implementation of this pattern already in the codebase.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#corollary-collection-defaults","title":"Corollary \u2014 Collection defaults","text":"<p>Collection-typed fields on domain objects default to the appropriate empty collection (<code>[]</code>, <code>{}</code>, <code>set()</code>), not <code>None</code>. Use <code>field(default_factory=list)</code> etc. in Pydantic models and dataclasses. <code>None</code> is reserved for fields where absence is semantically distinct from empty (e.g. AS2 fields where <code>None</code> omits the key from the wire payload).</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#corollary-bt-node-helpers-raise-update-catches","title":"Corollary \u2014 BT node helpers raise; <code>update()</code> catches","text":"<p>BT node helper methods must either complete successfully or raise a domain exception (e.g. <code>BtNodePreconditionError</code>). They must not return <code>None</code> as a failure signal. The <code>update()</code> method is the single <code>try/except</code> handler that converts the exception to <code>Status.FAILURE</code> and sets <code>self.feedback_message</code>.</p> <pre><code># GOOD \u2014 helper raises; update() catches\ndef _read_case_obj(self, case_id: str) -&gt; VulnerabilityCase:\n    try:\n        obj = self.blackboard[case_id]\n    except KeyError:\n        raise BtNodePreconditionError(f\"case {case_id!r} not in blackboard\")\n    if not is_case_model(obj):\n        raise BtNodePreconditionError(\n            f\"blackboard entry {case_id!r} is not a VulnerabilityCase\"\n        )\n    return obj\n\ndef update(self, ...) -&gt; Status:\n    try:\n        case_obj = self._read_case_obj(case_id)\n        ...\n    except BtNodePreconditionError as e:\n        self.feedback_message = str(e)\n        return Status.FAILURE\n</code></pre> <p>This eliminates the class of bug where a helper returns <code>None</code> silently with no <code>self.feedback_message</code> set.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0032-validate-at-edge-promote-to-core/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: stack traces point to the origin of core helpers.</li> <li>Good: eliminates <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate at call-sites.</li> <li>Good: aligns BT node helpers with the <code>dl.read()</code> precedent.</li> <li>Bad: requires migration of existing code; tracked in #1359 and #1360.</li> <li>Good: <code>BtNodePreconditionError</code> is now defined in <code>vultron/errors.py</code> and   importable as Core functions that require a case to have reached a particular stage (e.g. \"there is an active embargo\") cannot express that requirement in their type signatures, so they fall back on runtime guards (<code>if case.active_embargo is None: ...</code>, <code>if case.current_status.em_state == EM.ACTIVE: ...</code>).</p> <p>The Idea (#1362) proposed distinct types per lifecycle stage \u2014 illustratively <code>IncomingReport</code>, <code>TriagedCase</code>, <code>ActiveCase</code> \u2014 so a core function accepting a stage-specific type would reject earlier-stage data at the type level, with no <code>if x is None</code> needed. Each Actor is an isolated process: it owns a DataLayer of core domain objects, and (per the Actor Knowledge Model) its knowledge of the world is bounded strictly by what it has received. No actor can reach into another actor's DataLayer. Wire (AS2) exists solely as the transport by which one actor's core state informs another's \u2014 an AS2 Activity is an envelope carrying a core domain fact across the process boundary, not a domain object in its own right.</p> <p>ADR-0017 established that wire is a projection of core, and ARCH-09-001 requires core models to be as rich as or richer than their wire counterparts. The 29 AS2 protocol Activities (<code>Offer</code>, <code>Invite</code>, <code>Accept</code>, <code>Reject</code>, \u2026) break this: they were built wire-first and were never given a core counterpart. For these types the projection is inverted \u2014 wire is the only representation, and is therefore richer than core.</p> <p>The concrete consequence: when an actor must remember what a message told it (the case id an <code>Invite</code> carried, the recommender an <code>Offer</code> named, the report embedded in a submit <code>Offer</code>, the pending embargo proposal for a case), there is no core object to hold that fact, so core reaches back through the DataLayer and re-reads the stored wire envelope \u2014 <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> inside <code>vultron/core/</code>. Concern #1506 audited these sites. ADR-0034 recognised activity read-back as a boundary violation but explicitly scoped it out and deferred it to a separate concern; this ADR is that concern's decision.</p> <p>The <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> call in core is a symptom. The root cause is a missing layer of core domain representation for protocol facts. A second, subtler question surfaced during analysis: emitting a reply (e.g. an <code>Accept</code>) requires the full inline verbatim original activity in the reply's <code>object_</code> (the Actor Knowledge Model forbids bare URIs), and activity ids are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values \u2014 so the original envelope cannot be losslessly reconstructed from core state. Does that legitimise reading a stored activity back?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Restore \"wire is a projection of core\" (ADR-0017) and ARCH-09-001: every   domain fact an actor remembers MUST have a home in core.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-03-001 (AS2\u2194domain mapping happens in exactly one place, the   semantic extractor) \u2014 core MUST NOT re-interpret an activity a second time.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-01-002 / DL-05: wire vocabulary types MUST NOT enter core through   the persistence port.</li> <li>Do not regress into cloning each AS2 Activity into a 1:1 core Activity class \u2014   the generic-event-mirroring-AS2 anti-pattern <code>notes/domain-model-separation.md</code>   warns against.</li> <li>Satisfy the Actor Knowledge Model's requirement that replies embed the full   inline original activity, given that activity ids are not regenerable.</li> <li>Keep the migration measurable and regression-proof via the DL-05-004 ratchet.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. Give protocol facts a core representation; correlate via core entities;   confine verbatim reconstitution to a wire/adapter seam. The extractor   records the domain fact each inbound message carries as core state (a   transition on an existing core entity or a purpose-built core record) at   interpretation time. Core reads that core state; correlation between messages   (Accept\u2192Invite) flows through a core-entity relationship. Verbatim envelope   reconstitution for replies reads a stored activity back only through a   wire/adapter-owned seam that treats the payload as opaque.</li> <li>B. Clone each AS2 Activity into a 1:1 core Activity class. Give every   protocol message a mirror core type and read that instead. Rejected: this   duplicates the wire envelope into core rather than modelling the domain fact,   reproduces AS2-shaped fields (<code>object_</code>, <code>target</code>, <code>context</code>) in core   vocabulary, and is the exact anti-pattern <code>notes/domain-model-separation.md</code>   cautions against. It relocates the violation without curing it.</li> <li>C. Pure read-relocation / lossless re-projection. Stop storing activities;   reconstruct any needed envelope by re-projecting core state through the   serializer on demand. Rejected: activity ids are random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values, so   re-projection produces a different id and serialization every time \u2014 it cannot   reproduce the verbatim original the Actor Knowledge Model requires for reply   <code>object_</code>. That stream travels over a transport with no ordering guarantee, and Vultron may not be the only protocol implementation on the wire, so a replica can receive an entry before its hash-chain predecessor arrives.</p> <p>The original receive path (<code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>) treated any entry whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> did not match the local tail as a divergence: it dropped the entry and sent a <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> so the CaseActor would replay the missing prefix. At case closure this stalled a late-joining replica (Vendor2 in the FVV/FVCV demos) indefinitely and <code>wait_for_contiguous_ledger_coverage</code> timed out (issue #1556). How should a replica handle an entry that is valid but arrives before its predecessor?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Convergence must not depend on <code>Announce</code> delivery order (SYNC-10-004 requires   a contiguous prefix; the transport does not provide ordering).</li> <li>The fix must interoperate with unknown implementations \u2014 we cannot assume the   sender retries, or that any recovery message is delivered in order either.</li> <li>Must preserve the effects-before-persist invariant (SYNC-12-001) and the   DataLayer-presence-means-committed invariant (SYNC-13-001).</li> <li>Bounded memory under a broken or hostile peer that streams far-future entries.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. Repairing replay narrows the race but cannot close it under adversarial reordering. Buffering, by contrast, makes convergence order-independent: any valid entry is retained until the entry that closes its gap arrives, then drained in order.</p> <p>Buffering also makes the existing <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> recovery order-robust for free, because replayed entries flow through the same (now buffering) receive path. We therefore did not redesign the replay loop; we keep sending the <code>Reject</code> at buffer time purely as the backstop for entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. A companion correctness fix makes <code>SyncActivityAdapter.send_reject_log_entry</code> enqueue against the explicit receiving <code>actor_id</code> (like the announce path) instead of the DataLayer's own scope, so the Reject is delivered correctly even from a shared or differently-scoped DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: a late-joining replica converges to a contiguous prefix within a few   seconds of the tail arriving, regardless of <code>Announce</code> order (SYNC-10-004).</li> <li>Good: no new dependence on sender retry behavior \u2014 robust against other   implementations and lossy/reordering transports.</li> <li>Good: the buffer is a non-ledger holding area (SYNC-13-003), so the   \"DataLayer presence \u21d2 committed + effects applied\" invariant is preserved.</li> <li>Neutral: buffered state is in-memory and lost on restart; This level is covered by the wire format specifications. L2 \u2014 Semantic Correct state transitions in response to received messages and local events.   This level is covered by the Vultron Protocol spec (VP) and the   Transition Functions. L3 \u2014 Behavioral <p>Correct observable outputs \u2014 the right messages emitted and the right states reached   in response to a given (input state + received message/event) combination. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Activities are the core of the ActivityPub protocol. They are used to represent actions that are performed by actors. The ActivityStreams vocabulary defines a number of activities, and we extend these with specific activities that are used in the Vultron AS vocabulary. So far, we have found the ActivityStreams vocabulary to be sufficient for our needs, so our extensions are limited to specifying the types of activities, actors, and objects that are used in the Vultron protocol.</p> <p>A full mapping of Vultron to ActivityStreams is available in the Vultron ActivityStreams Ontology.</p> <p>Design Goals</p> <p>Our goal in each of these activity definitions is to</p> <ul> <li>Avoid creating new activity types when an existing activity type can be used.</li> <li>Avoid creating defined activity types with the same objects and targets to avoid confusion. Each activity type / object / target combination should have a single meaning within the protocol.</li> </ul> <p>For documentation purposes, we have divided the Vultron AS activities by user flow. Each of these user flows shows the activities that are used to perform a specific task. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Read</code></li> <li><code>as:View</code></li> <li><code>as:Listen</code></li> </ul> <p>Since most CVD cases are text-centric, we expect that the <code>as:Read</code> activity will be the most commonly used. However, we also expect that the <code>as:View</code> and <code>as:Listen</code> activities could be used in some cases, such as when a case participant views a video or listens to an audio recording.</p> <p>We specifically defined <code>RmReadReport</code> as a subclass of <code>as:Read</code> to indicate that a report has been read. This allows the receiver of a report to acknowledge receipt without indicating anything more than that the report has been read. That leaves <code>RmValidateReport</code> and <code>RmInvalidateReport</code> to indicate a more specific action (accept, reject) on the part of the receiver.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n    subgraph RM:Received\n        a{Accept?}\n        subgraph as:Read\n            RmReadReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Start\n        subgraph as:Offer\n            RmSubmitReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Accepted\n        subgraph as:Accept\n            RmValidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Invalid\n        subgraph as:Reject\n            RmInvalidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    a --&gt;|y| RmValidateReport\n    a --&gt;|undecided| RmReadReport\n    a --&gt;|n| RmInvalidateReport\n    RmSubmitReport --&gt; a</code></pre> <p>More Acknowledgements in the Ontology</p> <p>The Vultron AS ontology defines a number of ActivityStreams activities that can serve as the various acknowledgements that are used in the Vultron protocol. These include messages that are specifically <code>as:inReplyTo</code> a message defined as one of the core protocol message types.</p> <p>For example, it is not necessary to send a separate <code>RmReadReport</code> message if the <code>RmValidateReport</code> message is sent as a reply to the <code>RmSubmitReport</code> message. The <code>RmValidateReport</code> message logically indicates that the report has been read in order to have been validated.</p> <p>Like, Dislike and Flag</p> <p>The ActivityStreams vocabulary also includes actions that indicate an opinion  about a message or object, such as <code>as:Like</code>, <code>as:Dislike</code>, and <code>as:Flag</code>. While these may be relevant to implementations of the Vultron protocol, we do not have specific use cases for them at this time.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/acknowledge/#demo","title":"Demo","text":"<p>Try it: <code>vultron-demo acknowledge</code></p> <p>Run this workflow end-to-end with the unified demo CLI:</p> <pre><code>vultron-demo acknowledge\n</code></pre> <p>Or with Docker Compose:</p> <pre><code>DEMO=acknowledge docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm demo\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/error/","title":"Error Handling","text":"<p>While the ActivityStreams vocabulary doesn't include any specific error messages, we can use the <code>as:Reject</code> activity to indicate that a message has been rejected for some reason. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>The process to establish an embargo for a case can start in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li>Any participant can propose an embargo for a case. This is the most common   way to establish an embargo.</li> <li>The case owner can add an embargo to a case without proposing it first. In some circumstances, this might be an   appropriate way to establish an embargo.</li> </ul> <p></p> <p>Embargo Management in Vultron</p> <p>The Vultron protocol contains quite a bit of detail about Embargo Management and how participants are expected to interact with embargoes. Please refer to that section for more information.</p> <p>Why would you add an embargo without asking first?</p> <p>There are a few reasons why you might want to add an embargo to a case without asking first. For example, when the finder is also the case owner and hasn't invited any other participants to join the case yet, the finder can just add an embargo. Then when the finder invites others to join the case, the invited participants can decide whether to accept the embargo or not. This could be an appropriate way to address the concept of Default Embargoes.</p> <pre><code>flowchart TB\n    subgraph as:Invite\n        EmProposeEmbargo\n    end\n    subgraph as:Question\n <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Inviting an actor to a case is a way to add them as a participant in the case. The invitation is sent to the actor as an <code>as:Invite</code> activity. Depending on the actor's response, they may become a participant in the case.</p> <p> </p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Invite Actor to Case\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor O as Case Owner\n    actor A as Actor\n    participant C as Case\n    activate O\n    O -&gt;&gt;+ A: Invite(actor=CaseOwner, object=Actor, target=Case)\n    note over A: Consider invitation\n    alt Accept Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; O: Accept(object=Invite)\n        alt Create CaseParticipant\n        O -&gt;&gt; C: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        else Add CaseParticipant\n        O -&gt;&gt; O: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor))\n        O -&gt;&gt; C: Add(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        end\n        note over C: Actor becomes participant in case\n    else Reject Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; O: Reject(object=Invite)\n        note over C: Actor is not participant in case\n    end\n    deactivate A\n    deactivate O</code></pre> <p>Invite vs Add?</p> <p>When a case is first created, the Case Owner and any known participants (e.g., the Reporter) should be automatically added to the case. It's not even necessary for these to be emitted as separate <code>as:Add</code> activities. The <code>as:Create</code> activity for the case can include the Case Owner and any known participants as <code>CaseParticipant</code> objects. See Initializing a Case for more.</p> <p>However, over the lifespan of a case, there may be other actors that were not already involved at the time the case was created, but who should be invited to participate in the case. This is where the <code>as:Invite</code> activity comes in.</p> <p>Avoid bogging down in details</p> <p>Adding a participant to a case involves creating the participant object and a participant status object. As we discuss elsewhere, it's probably overkill to emit separate <code>as:Create</code> and <code>as:Add</code> events for each of these events.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n\na[create participant] for the participant, already containing a status object, and have the <code>target</code> of the <code>as:Create</code> event be the case object.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\na[create particpant with We chose to  represent them separately here to acknowledge the difference between creating a new object and adding an existing object to another object, but in an actual implementation it may be acceptable to use either activity for both cases. It seems likely that the general idea should be to use <code>as:Create</code> when creating a new object to  add to another object (as the <code>target</code> of the activity), and <code>as:Add</code> when adding an existing object to another object. </p> <p>That said, our intent is that Vultron be consistent with however ActivityPub does this. core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Case","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>During the course of coordinating a case, an existing case participant might recognize that another actor should be invited to participate in the case. The following mechanisms provide a way for a case participant to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case.</p> <p> </p> <p>Why Suggest instead of just Invite?</p> <p>The process described here makes an assumption that there is a case owner who is responsible for coordinating the  case. Participants having the case owner role can in principle just directly invite other actors to participate in  the case, and they might not need the suggestion mechanism described here. However, we include this mechanism to account for the possibilities that:</p> <ul> <li>there could be multiple case owners, and they might not all agree on who should be invited to participate in the    case.</li> <li>a non-case-owner participant might want to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case</li> </ul> <p>Of these, the latter is the more likely scenario, but the mechanism described here can be used in either case.    </p> <p>Reasons to Invite other Actors</p> <p>There are many reasons why a case participant might want to suggest another actor to participate in a case. The following are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder, having reported to one vendor, might further discover that the vulnerability is actually in a    third-party library, and suggest inviting the library vendor to participate in the case.</li> <li>A vendor might be a participant in (but not the owner of) a case, and wants to suggest that the case owner   invite a sector-specific coordinator to participate in the case to address critical infrastructure concerns.</li> <li>A reporter participant might suggest a technical expert (for example, a member of a protocol working group) to    include in the case.</li> <li>A coordinator might suggest to the case owner that a large deployer be invited to participat in a case to    address concerns about the impact of deploying a fix for a vulnerability on infrastructure and operations.</li> </ul> <p>Below is a sequence diagram showing the process of suggesting an actor for a case. We used a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Suggesting an Actor for a Case (ADR-0026 CaseActor-routed)\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Recommender\n    participant CA as CaseActor\n    actor B as Case Owner\n    actor D as Invitee\n    Note over A: Recognize that Actor should be invited\n    A -&gt;&gt; CA: Offer(object=Actor, target=Case)\n    activate CA\n    Note over CA: Record in ledger, assign default roles\n    CA -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=CaseParticipant{actor,roles}, target=Case, origin=Offer.id)\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: AcceptActorRecommendation\n        CA -&gt;&gt;+ D: Invite(CaseStub + embargo + roles)\n        note over D: Respond to invitation (not shown)\n        deactivate D\n    else Reject Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: RejectActorRecommendation\n    end\n    deactivate B\n    deactivate CA</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/suggest_actor/#recommend-actor","title":"Recommend Actor","text":"<p>A participant recommends another actor to the CaseActor by sending an <code>Offer</code> activity with the <code>object</code> property set to the actor being recommended and the <code>target</code> set to the case. core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Transfer if case ownership was not part of the original Vultron protocol, but it seems like a reasonable extension that could be useful in some cases, such as transferring a case</p> <ul> <li>from a researcher to a vendor</li> <li>from a vendor to an upstream vendor</li> <li>from a vendor to a coordinator</li> <li>from a coordinator to a vendor</li> <li>between coordinators</li> </ul> <p>The presumption here is that the initial creator of a case is its owner. Subsequent to that, the existing owner can offer to transfer ownership to another participant. The new owner can then accept or reject the offer.</p> <p>We use a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>sequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Current Case Owner\n    actor B as Potential Case Owner\n    participant C as Case\n    A -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=Case)\n    note over B: Consider offer\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Offer\n        B --&gt;&gt; A: Accept(object=Offer)\n        A -&gt;&gt; C: Update(object=Case)\n        note over C: Case has new owner\n    else Reject Offer\n        B --&gt;&gt; A: Reject(object=Offer)\n        note over C: Case ownership unchanged\n    end\n    deactivate B</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/transfer_ownership/#offer-case-ownership-transfer","title":"Offer Case Ownership Transfer","text":"<p>The current owner of a case can offer simplifies consistency guarantees and avoids concurrent-write conflicts Single leader, master authority Canonical Recorded Log The authoritative append-only history maintained by the CaseActor; hash-chained for verification; replicated to Participants via <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> messages Authoritative log, master log Case Ledger Entry A single item in the canonical recorded log; includes a trusted timestamp generated by the CaseActor (never copied from inbound Activities), hash of its content, and hash of its predecessor (forming a Merkle chain) Log item, journal entry Eventual Consistency The replication guarantee that Participant replicas converge to the CaseActor's state as Case Ledger Entries are delivered and processed Convergence property Participant Case Replica A local copy of VulnerabilityCase state maintained by a Participant node; What exactly is a process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Each Participant in a Case runs one Process. A Process maintains a Composite State \u2014 that's a 3-tuple: (Case State, RM State, EM State).\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"So if a Vendor is in the case, they're one Process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Exactly. The Vendor runs their own RM state machine, tracks the shared EM state, and maintains their part of the Case State (Vendor Fix Path). Meanwhile, a Coordinator in the same Case is another Process with their own RM state and the same EM state.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"And they coordinate through Message Types?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Yes. When a Vendor transitions their RM from Valid to Accepted, they send an RA (Report Accepted) Message Type. That Activity carries the RA and is transmitted via the wire protocol. The Coordinator receives it and updates their model of the Vendor's RM State.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"But that doesn't change the Coordinator's own RM state?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Correct. The RA message is an announcement \u2014 'I accepted the report.' It doesn't command the receiver to do anything. Only Report Submission (RS) directly changes receiver RM state.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"What about CS Events \u2014 if the Vendor completes a fix, do they have to send a message?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Not technically. The Vendor internal transitions from Vfd to VFd is a CS Event (F). But per the protocol, they SHOULD announce it by sending a CF (Fix Readiness) message. However, the message and the state transition are distinct \u2014 one doesn't require the other formally.\"</p>"},{"location":"reference/glossary/#architecture-example","title":"Architecture Example","text":"<p>Architect: \"OK, so our issue is that <code>vultron/core/use_cases/triggers/sync.py</code> calls <code>from_core()</code> \u2014 but <code>from_core()</code> is in the wire layer. That violates ARCH-03-001.\"</p> <p>Developer: \"Right, I see it: <code>CaseLedgerEntry.from_core(entry)</code>. Most activity in Vultron involves actors exchanging activity messages containing objects.</p> <p>Submitting a Vulnerability Report</p> <p>For example, an actor might create a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object and then offer it to another actor, who can then accept, tentatively reject, or  reject the offer.</p> <p>Actors in ActivityPub can be of various types, such as <code>Person</code>, <code>Organization</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Application</code>, <code>Service</code>, etc. Each actor has an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is where the actor receives activities, and the outbox is where the actor sends activities.</p> <p>Actor Inboxes and Outboxes</p> <p>For example, if Alice is a <code>Person</code> actor, she has an inbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/inbox</code> and an outbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/outbox</code>. If Bob is another <code>Person</code> actor, he has his own inbox and outbox.</p> <p>When Alice wants to send an activity to Bob, she creates the activity with the <code>to</code> field set to Bob's actor ID (e.g., <code>https://example.com/users/bob</code>) and places it in her outbox. The ActivityPub server then delivers the activity to Bob's inbox. Bob can then process the activity and respond by sending an activity to his outbox, with the <code>to</code> field set to Alice's actor ID. He can also set the <code>inReplyTo</code> field to reference the original activity from Alice to indicate that it is a response. The ActivityPub server handles the delivery of the activity to Alice's inbox,  and the cycle continues.</p> <p>Scope of Vultron's ActivityPub Implementation</p> <p>However, in our Vultron prototype, we are not implementing a full ActivityPub server. Instead, we're initially focusing on the core functionality of actors sending activities directly to each other's inboxes. This simplifies the implementation while still allowing us to demonstrate the core concepts of ActivityPub interactions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-architecture","title":"Inbox Handler Architecture","text":"<p>Our initial architecture is as follows: An actor has an inbox implemented as a FastAPI endpoint that accepts POST requests containing activity messages. If the validation failed, it can respond with an appropriate error status (e.g., 400 Bad Request) and log the error.</li> <li>Extract Routing Information: The inbox handler extracts key fields from the activity message (e.g., <code>type</code>, <code>object</code>, <code>to</code>, <code>inReplyTo</code>) to determine routing. This decouples the raw activity message structure from the higher-level semantics of the Vultron protocol, allowing us to translate raw messages into meaningful semantics that drive application logic.</p> <p>Defining Activity Patterns</p> <p>We might define an activity pattern for submitting a vulnerability report as an <code>Offer</code> activity with an object of type <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>. The handler function is then invoked with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object as an argument.</p> <p>Example</p> <p>The following is an example of the <code>ActivityDispatcher</code> Protocol that defines   the interface for dispatching activities:</p> <pre><code>class ActivityDispatcher(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\n    Protocol for dispatching activities to their corresponding handlers based on message semantics.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def dispatch(self, dispatchable: DispatchEvent) -&gt; None:\n        \"\"\"Dispatches an activity to the appropriate handler based on its semantic type.\"\"\"\n        ...\n</code></pre> <p>On the Modularity of Dispatchers</p> <p>The dispatch function is designed as a Python <code>Protocol</code> to allow for different dispatcher implementations. This provides flexibility in connecting the inbox  handler to specific handler functions for each semantic type. A simple  implementation might use a dictionary mapping from semantic types to handler  functions, while a more complex implementation could involve message queues  or other routing mechanisms.</p> <p>This modularity allows us to easily extend dispatching logic by defining new  <code>ActivityPattern</code>s with corresponding <code>MessageSemantics</code>, then adding new  handler functions to the dispatch mapping. By decoupling routing logic from  handling logic, we maintain clean separation of concerns and facilitate  future protocol extensions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#direct-dispatch-implementation","title":"Direct Dispatch Implementation","text":"<p>Our first dispatch function implementation uses a simple direct dispatch approach with a dictionary mapping from <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. Thus, a value of Credible can be expected to lead to an RM transition to Valid (\\(q^{rm} \\in R \\xrightarrow{v} V\\)), assuming any additional validation checks also pass. From the Coordinator's perspective, if enough Suppliers in a CVD case have communicated their engagement in a case (i.e., enough Vendors are in the RM Accepted state already or are expected to make it there soon from either the Received or Valid states), then the SSVC value would be Active.</p> <p>Vendors in Invalid or Closed can be taken as disengaged, and it might be appropriate to select Unresponsive for the SSVC Engagement decision point.</p> <p>Vendors in either Received or Deferred might be either Active or Unresponsive, depending on the specific report history.</p> <p>This mapping is formalized below and in the figure that follows.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Engagement Decision Point Mapped to RM States</p> \\[ SSVC(supp.~eng.) =  \\begin{cases}     Active &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\} \\\\     \\\\     \\begin{cases}         Active \\\\         Unresponsive     \\end{cases} &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{R,D\\} \\\\     \\\\     Unresponsive &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{I,C,S\\} \\\\ \\end{cases}\\] <pre><code>---\ntitle: \"RM States and SSVC Supplier Engagement\"\n---\ngraph LR\n    subgraph ssvc_se[SSVC Supplier Engagement]\n        Active\n        Unresponsive\n    end\n    subgraph rm_states[RM States]\n        S[Start]\n        R[Received]\n        I[Invalid]\n        V[Valid]\n        D[Deferred]\n        A[Accepted]\n        C[Closed]\n    end\n    A --&gt; Active\n    V --&gt; Active\n    R --&gt; Active\n    D --&gt; Active\n    R--&gt; Unresponsive\n    D --&gt; Unresponsive\n    I --&gt; Unresponsive\n    C --&gt; Unresponsive\n    S --&gt; Unresponsive</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/ssvc_crosswalk/#supplier-involvement","title":"Supplier Involvement","text":"<p>The Supplier Involvement decision point can take on the values Fix-Ready, Cooperative, or Uncooperative/Unresponsive. We begin by noting the equivalence of the Fix-Ready value with the similarly named substate of the CS model.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Involvement Decision Point Mapped to CS States</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     SSVC(supp.~inv.) = Fix~Ready \\iff q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot \\end{aligned}\\] <p>The Vendor RM states map onto these values as formalized below and shown in the figure below.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Involvement Decision Point Mapped to Vendor RM States</p> \\[\\begin{aligned} SSVC(supp.~inv.) =  \\begin{cases}     \\begin{cases}         Fix~Ready \\\\         Cooperative     \\end{cases} &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in A \\\\     \\\\     Cooperative &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in V \\\\     \\\\     Uncoop./Unresp. &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{R,I,D,C,S\\} \\\\ \\end{cases} \\end{aligned}\\] <pre><code>---\ntitle: \"RM States and SSVC Supplier Involvement\"\n---\ngraph LR\n    subgraph rm_states[RM States]\n        S[Start]\n        R[Received]\n        I[Invalid]\n        V[Valid]\n        D[Deferred]\n        A[Accepted]\n        C[Closed]\n    end\n\n    subgraph ssvc_si[SSVC Supplier Involvement]\n        fr[Fix-Ready]\n        co[Cooperative]\n        un[Uncooperative/Unresponsive]\n    end\n    A --&gt; fr\n    A --&gt; co\n    V --&gt; co\n    R --&gt; un\n    D --&gt; un\n    I --&gt; un\n    C --&gt; un\n    S --&gt; un</code></pre> <p>Engagement vs. Involvement: What's the Difference?</p> <p>Note the discrepancy between the mappings given for SSVC Supplier Engagement versus those for Supplier Involvement. This distinction is most prominent in the connections from the Received and Deferred RM states in the two figures above. These differences are the result of the relative timing of the two different decisions they support within a CVD case.</p> <p>The decision to Coordinate (i.e., whether the Coordinator should move from RM Valid to RM Accept  (\\(q^{rm} \\in V \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) occurs early in the Coordinator's RM process. The SSVC Supplier Engagement decision point is an attempt to capture this information. This early in the process, allowances must be made for Vendors who may not have completed their own validation or  prioritization processes.  Hence, the mapping allows Vendors in any valid yet unclosed state (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{R,V,A,D\\}\\)) to be categorized as  Active for this decision point.</p> <p>On the other hand, the decision to Publish\u2014a choice that falls entirely within the Coordinator's RM Accepted  state\u2014occurs later, at which time, more is known about each Vendor's level of involvement in the case to that point.  By the time the publication decision is made, the Vendor(s) have had ample opportunity to engage in the CVD process. They might already have a Fix-Ready (\\(q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\)), or they might be working toward it (i.e., SSVC Cooperative). However, if the Coordinator has reached the point where they are making a publication decision, and the Vendor has  yet to actively engage in the case for whatever reason\u2014as indicated by their failure to reach the RM Accepted state or demonstrate progress toward it by at least getting to RM Valid  (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\}\\))\u2014then they can be categorized as Uncooperative/Unresponsive.</p> <p>SSVC Decision Points and Anticipated Transitions</p> <p>Other SSVC decision points may be informative about which transitions to expect in a case. Two examples apply here:</p> <ol> <li>Supplier Engagement acts to gauge the likelihood of the F transitions. Coordination becomes more necessary the lower that likelihood is.</li> <li>Utility (the usefulness of the exploit to the adversary) acts to gauge the likelihood of the A transition.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/terms/","title":"Terms and Definitions","text":"<p>Throughout this documentation, we refer to CVD Roles from the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure:</p> <p>Finder</p> <p>The individual or organization that identifies the vulnerability</p> <p>Reporter</p> <p>The individual or organization that notifies the vendor of the vulnerability</p> <p>Vendor (Supplier)</p> <p>The individual or organization that created or maintains the vulnerable product</p> <p>The Vendor role is synonymous with the Supplier role as it appears in SSVC Version 2 and above.</p> <p>Deployer (User)</p> <p>The individual or organization that must deploy a patch or take other remediation action</p> <p>The Deployer role is synonymous with the User role in ISO/IEC 29147:2018 and ISO/IEC 30111:2019, while the other roles are named consistent with those standards.</p> <p>Coordinator</p> <p>An individual or organization that facilitates the coordinated response process</p> <p>We also add a new role in this documentation, which we expect to incorporate into a future version of the CVD Guide:</p> <p>Exploit Publisher</p> <p>An individual or organization that publishes exploits</p> <p>Exploit Publishers might be the same as Finders, Reporters, Coordinators, or Vendors, but this is not guaranteed. Implementations of the Vultron Protocol are expected to have their own versioning schemes.</p> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev3641+g6903494aa</p> <p>Vultron Protocol versions follow Calendar Versioning (CalVer) using the format <code>YYYY.M.Patch</code>, where:</p> <ul> <li> <p><code>YYYY</code> is the four-digit year of the most recent non-patch release.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>M</code> is the month of the most recent non-patch release,     with no zero padding (e.g., <code>1</code>, <code>2</code>, <code>3</code>, ..., <code>12</code>).</p> </li> <li> <p><code>Patch</code> is the patch number for that release.     For the first (or only) release in a given month, the patch number     starts at <code>0</code> and is normally omitted, so <code>2024.4.0</code> and <code>2024.4</code>     denote the same version.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Version increments work as follows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Significant releases use the current year and month, with the patch     number starting at <code>0</code> (normally omitted).     Example: the first significant release in April 2024 is <code>2024.4</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Patch releases increment the patch number from the most recent     non-patch release, even if the patch is published in a later month or year.     Example: the third small update to <code>2024.4</code> is <code>2024.4.3</code>, even if it     is released in May 2024 or later.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Because we are still in the early stages of the project, no backward compatibility commitments are made or implied at this time. We anticipate this will change as the protocol matures.</p>"},{"location":"reference/case_states/","title":"Index","text":""},{"location":"reference/case_states/#case-states","title":"Case This design allows us to separate the core domain logic from the infrastructure and external interfaces, making the system more modular, testable, and adaptable to different use cases and environments.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Overview\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nadapters1[Driving Adapters]\nadapters2[Driven Adapters]\nports1[Driving Ports]\nports2[Driven Ports]\ncore{{Core Domain Logic}}\nadapters1 --o ports1\nports1 --o core\ncore --o ports2\nports2 --o adapters2</code></pre> <p>In this architecture:</p> <ul> <li>The Driving Adapters implement the driving ports using specific   technologies (e.g., FastAPI endpoints, CLI commands, etc.) and translate   external inputs into calls to the core domain logic.</li> <li>The Driving Ports define the interfaces through which external actors   (e.g., finders, vendors, coordinators) can interact with the core domain logic. These are the entry points for commands and queries that drive the system's behavior.</li> <li>The Core Domain Logic contains the business rules, policies, and behavior trees that govern how the system operates. It is completely agnostic to how it is accessed or what technologies are used to implement the interfaces.</li> <li>The Driven Ports define the interfaces through which the core domain   logic can interact with external systems (e.g., databases, message queues,   external APIs). These are the exit points for the core to perform actions   that have side effects or require external resources.</li> <li>The Driven Adapters implement the driven ports using specific technologies   (e.g., MongoDB for database access, Celery for task queues, etc.)   and   translate calls from the core domain logic into interactions with external   systems.</li> </ul> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Details\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nsubgraph driving_adapters [Driving Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    api[API Endpoints]\n    cli[CLI Commands]\n    mcp[MCP Tools]\nend\nsubgraph driving_ports [Driving Ports]\n    direction LR\n    use_cases[Use Cases]\n    commands[Commands]\nend\nsubgraph core [Core Domain Logic]\n    direction LR\n    domain_models[Domain Models]\n    services[Domain Services]\n    behavior_trees[Behavior Trees]\nend\nsubgraph driven_ports [Driven Ports]\n    direction LR\n    database[Database Access]\n    message_queue[Message Queue]\n    external_apis[External APIs]\nend\nsubgraph driven_adapters [Driven Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    mongo[MongoDB Adapter]\n    celery[Celery Adapter]\n    vince[VINCE Adapter]\nend\n\ndriving_adapters --&gt; driving_ports\ndriving_ports --&gt; core\ncore --&gt; driven_ports\ndriven_ports --&gt; driven_adapters</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/code/api/actor_inbox_handler/","title":"Actor Inbox Handler","text":"<p>The Actor Inbox Handler is the hub that processes incoming activities. It</p> <ul> <li>receives activities sent to an actor's inbox</li> <li>looks up the appropriate handler based on the activity type and object type</li> <li>invokes the handler to process the activity</li> <li>if necessary, delegates to sub-handlers for more specific processing</li> </ul> <p>Some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> handlers have more than one job</p> <p>For some <code>Activity</code>/<code>Object</code> pairs, there may be multiple jobs to select from. For example, handling an <code>Accept(Invite(VulnerabilityCase))</code> activity is different from handling an <code>Accept(Invite(Embargo))</code> activity. In such cases, the Actor Inbox Handler will invoke a handler for the Accept(Invite) activity, which will then delegate to the appropriate sub-handler based on the details of the offer being accepted.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Actor Inbox Handler\n---\nflowchart TB\n\nsource[client]\nsubgraph Actor\n  inbox\nend\nsubgraph handler\n  func[ActivityType,&lt;br/&gt;ObjectType]\nend\nsource --&gt;|1. POST| inbox\ninbox --&gt;|2. async| handler\ninbox --&gt;|3. response| source\nregistry(Handler&lt;br/&gt;Registry)\nhandler &lt;--&gt;|4. lookup| registry\nhdlrA[handler actor_id,activity]\nhandler happening, or has already happened. The Activity type itself serves as an abstract base type for all types of activities. It is important to note that an Activity is not a representation of a currently executing process, but rather a statement about that process. For example, a person walking down the street is not an Activity unless they are posting a picture of themselves walking down the street. The maximum failures is then calculated as <code>N - m</code>, where N is the number of children.</p> <ul> <li>When a child returns SUCCESS, the ParallelNode increments a success counter.</li> <li>When a child returns FAILURE, the ParallelNode increments a failure counter.</li> <li>If the success counter reaches the minimum number of successes, the ParallelNode returns SUCCESS.</li> <li>If the failure counter reaches the maximum number of failures, the ParallelNode returns FAILURE.</li> <li>If neither of the above conditions are met, the ParallelNode returns RUNNING.</li> </ul> <p>Not Fully Implemented</p> <p>In the current implementation, the ParallelNode does not actually tick its children in parallel. and runs it until either it closes or 1000 ticks have passed. This demo is basically simulating a CVD agent coordinating a CVD case with itself. The agent's role is set to <code>FINDER_REPORTER_VENDOR_DEPLOYER_COORDINATOR</code>, which means it will perform all the roles in the CVD case. Messages emitted in one tick might be received later in the same tick, or in a future tick.</p> <p>Tip</p> <p>This demo leverages the ability to use leaf nodes as stochastic process fuzzers.  Using this feature, we can simulate the behavior of a CVD agent without having to  implement any actual communication mechanisms or simulate any complex real-world processes.</p> <p>One interesting effect of this design is that the places where the demo uses a fuzzer node are often  indicative of places where an actual bot would either need to call out to either a data source or  a human to decide what to do next. This is a good example of how the Vultron behavior tree  can be used to model complex reactive processes in a way that is still easy to understand and reason about.</p> <p>Note</p> <p>There is no underlying communication mechanism in this demo, so messages are not actually  sent anywhere. Instead, they are just added to the blackboard's incoming message queue.  They also have no content, and are only represented as message types.</p> <p>Warning</p> <p>This demo is not intended to be a fully realistic simulation of a CVD case. It is only intended  to demonstrate the behavior of the Vultron behavior tree.</p>"},{"location":"reference/code/demo/","title":"Demo Package","text":"<p>The <code>vultron.demo</code> package contains Brand and Zafiropulo defined a protocol as follows.</p> <p>Protocol Formally Defined</p> <p>A protocol with \\(N\\) processes is a quadruple:</p> \\[ protocol =      \\Big \\langle          { \\langle S_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},          { \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},         { \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle}^N_{i,j=1},         { succ }     \\Big \\rangle\\] <p>Where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(N\\) is a positive integer representing the number of processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle S_i \\rangle_{i=1}^N\\) are \\(N\\) disjoint finite sets (\\(S_i\\) represents the set of states of process \\(i\\)).</p> </li> <li> <p>Each \\(o_i\\) is an element of \\(S_i\\) representing the initial state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\). \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\),</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(succ\\) is a partial function mapping for each \\(i\\) and \\(j\\), $\\(S_i \\times M_{ij} \\rightarrow S_i \\textrm{ and } S_i \\times M_{ji} \\rightarrow S_i\\)$ \\(succ(s,x)\\) is the state entered after a process transmits or receives message \\(x\\) in state \\(s\\). It is a transmission if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ij}\\) and a reception if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ji}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>Global State Formally Defined</p> <p>The global state of a protocol given by the above is a pair \\(\\langle S, C \\rangle\\), where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(S\\) is an \\(N\\)-tuple of states \\(\\langle s_1,\\dots,s_N \\rangle\\) with each \\(s_i\\) representing the current state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(C\\) is an \\(N^2\\)-tuple \\(\\langle c_{1,1},\\dots, c_{1,N}, c_{2,1}, \\dots \\dots, c_{N,N} \\rangle\\), where each \\(c_{i,j}\\) is a sequence of messages from \\(M_{i,j}\\). The message sequence \\(c_{i,j}\\) represents the contents of the channel from process \\(i\\) to \\(j\\). (Note that \\(c_{i,j}\\) is empty when \\(i = j\\) since processes are presumed to not communicate with themselves.)</p> </li> </ul> <p>We detail each of these below or in subsequent pages:</p> <ul> <li>\\(N\\) below</li> <li>\\({ \\langle S_i \\rangle}^N_{i=1}\\), and \\({ \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1}\\) in States,</li> <li>\\({ \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle }^N_{i,j=1}\\) in Message Types,</li> <li>\\({ succ }\\) in Transition Functions</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/#number-of-processes","title":"Number of Processes","text":"<p>The processes we are concerned with represent the different Participants in their roles (Finder, Vendor, Coordinator, Deployer, and Other).
