The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. OX-08-004 narrows its WARNING scope to exclude this purposeful self-copy pattern (the only valid use of <code>cc:</code> in the protocol).</p> <p>The working precedent for this pattern is <code>offer_case_manager_role</code>: its <code>ResolveCaseManagerOfferContextNode</code> sets <code>blackboard.offer_case_manager_to = [case_actor_id]</code> and the Offer is addressed to the CaseActor's own ID in <code>to:</code> (a special case where the CaseActor is genuinely the primary recipient). Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing","text":""},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This already satisfies the actor-identity   requirement; the fix here is purely \"move this tree into a named factory   function in <code>behaviors/case/</code>,\" not an actor-switching repair.</li> </ul> <p>All nine sites import <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> directly into <code>vultron/core/use_cases/</code>, which is what the structural test (below) detects \u2014 but the underlying defect, and the fix required, differs by category. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. Investigation found <code>receiving_actor_id</code> is already resolved before dispatch (<code>FastAPIDispatchAdapter.dispatch()</code>, which sets it from the canonical actor ID resolved off the inbox URL path) and is already present on every received-side event by the time <code>execute()</code> runs. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code>   BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree. The use case's tree-factory function composes the main operation subtree and the guarded-commit subtree (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>, or an equivalent Selector/Sequence/Success branch) as siblings or a sequence within one tree. Any identity referenced by the message other than <code>receiving_actor_id</code> (invitee, accepting actor, sender) is threaded into the tree as leaf-node constructor arguments or blackboard keys \u2014 data, not a second <code>actor_id</code>.</p> <p>Option B \u2014 Keep the current two-call shape; tighten only the pre-flight guard's correctness (status quo, amended). A Sentinel monitors a condition over time and fires a trigger endpoint when that condition is met.</p> <p>A node that queries an external system synchronously and returns only a binary (yes/no) result is still a Retriever: a boolean is the simplest possible structured fact. After FUZZ-01 through FUZZ-07 (#860\u2013#866), each call-out point has a probabilistic fuzzer node as its stand-in. The fuzzer is not a permanent implementation: it is an adapter that will be replaced over time by real data lookups, policy evaluations, or coordination agents.</p> <p>Before those replacements can happen, the call-out points must be expressed as proper injection seams: the BT tree must be built so that the fuzzer is the default backend, not the only option. Without an abstraction layer, swapping any call-out point requires finding and editing the concrete node class instead of injecting a different factory \u2014 and with roughly 93 call-out point nodes across all domains, the maintenance burden is unacceptable.</p> <p>The design question is: What mechanism makes each call-out point backend swappable while remaining consistent with the existing py_trees Behaviour pattern, factory-function conventions, and blackboard contract model?</p> <p>Design status \u2014 formed in sand, not concrete: This ADR captures the forward-looking intent after one planning session. The design will be exercised in #1151 (one exemplar per agent shape) and is expected to converge after two or three concrete implementations across different domain areas. Implementers working on the shape-based follow-on issues (FUZZ-08d through FUZZ-08g) SHOULD refine this ADR if the pattern proves incorrect or incomplete. The ADR status will advance from <code>proposed</code> to <code>accepted</code> once the exemplars validate the approach.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Must be consistent with the existing BT factory-function pattern   (tree composition functions, not ad-hoc node instantiation)</li> <li>Must allow individual call-out points to be swapped without changing the   calling tree structure (incremental replacement)</li> <li>Must maintain the same blackboard contract whether the backend is a fuzzer   or a real implementation \u2014 downstream nodes must be unaffected by the swap</li> <li>Must keep simulation artifacts (<code>vultron/demo/fuzzer/</code>) out of   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> (BT-16-001)</li> <li>Must be compatible with the four agent shapes from ADR-0024 (Sentinel,   Evaluator, Retriever, Composer), each of which has different input/output   semantics</li> <li>Must support partial replacement: a scenario can use real implementations   for some call-out points and fuzzer backends for others in the same run</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0025-call-out-point-abstraction-layer/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>No abstraction \u2014 leave fuzzer nodes as concrete hardcoded classes; <code>vultron/core/</code> are peppered with <code>if x is None: return None</code> chains. These silent failures propagate far from their source \u2014 the error surfaces at the point of use rather than the point of origin, making debugging difficult and creating a class of bug where program state is quietly corrupted or silently skipped.</p> <p>The root cause is structural: loose wire-layer types (where <code>Optional</code> fields are correct \u2014 AS2 permits many fields to be absent) leak directly into core logic without being promoted to tighter representations. Core functions then defensively guard every field they actually require.</p> <p>A secondary symptom is collection-typed fields and parameters that default to <code>None</code> instead of an empty collection, forcing every call-site to write <code>x or []</code> / <code>x or {}</code> boilerplate before iteration.</p> <p>The DataLayer already established the right precedent: <code>dl.read()</code> raises <code>VultronNotFoundError</code> rather than returning <code>None</code>. At the boundary (extractor, rehydration layer,    use-case entry point), required fields are validated. If absent, a    descriptive exception is raised immediately \u2014 not propagated as <code>None</code>.</li> <li>Core receives strict types. Changes","text":""},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p><code>VulnerabilityCase</code> is the canonical \"fat class\" named in ADR-0032: one type represents a case at every lifecycle stage. Core functions that require a case to have reached a particular stage (e.g. \"there is an active embargo\") cannot express that requirement in their type signatures, so they fall back on runtime guards (<code>if case.active_embargo is None: ...</code>, <code>if case.current_status.em_state == EM.ACTIVE: ...</code>).</p> <p>The Idea (#1362) proposed distinct types per lifecycle stage \u2014 illustratively <code>IncomingReport</code>, <code>TriagedCase</code>, <code>ActiveCase</code> \u2014 so a core function accepting a stage-specific type would reject earlier-stage data at the type level, with no <code>if x is None</code> needed. The Idea explicitly deferred deriving the actual stages from the protocol until a design was reviewed.</p> <p>Two protocol facts, verified against the code, shape the answer and make the naive \"one type per RM state\" framing unworkable:</p> <ol> <li>RM state is per-participant, not case-universal. Each <code>CaseParticipant</code>    runs its own RM state machine (<code>ParticipantStatus.rm_state</code>). There is no    such thing as \"the case is in RM.VALID\" \u2014 valid according to whom? A case    type named <code>ValidCase</code>/<code>TriagedCase</code> would be ill-defined.</li> <li>Only a few facts are genuinely case-universal. Case existence,    structural minimums (\u22651 report, reporter + receiver participants), the    embargo state (<code>EM</code>, one per case), and public state (<code>pxa</code>) are the only    monotonic facts that hold case-wide.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Make illegal shapes unrepresentable in core logic (ADR-0032 continuation).</li> <li>Do not introduce a type whose fields are identical to its parent's \u2014 that is   ceremony without a type-checker payoff and invites combinatorial proliferation   (2\u00b3 for the independent P/X/A dimensions alone).</li> <li>The design must survive DataLayer round-trip: rehydration always yields a   valid object, so the design must specify how a rehydrated record acquires its   staged type.</li> <li>Reuse the existing precedents: the role-specific <code>CaseParticipant</code> subclasses,   the <code>RM_ACTIVE</code> / <code>EM_NEGOTIATING</code> state-group tuples, and the   <code>is_rm_at_least()</code> predicate family.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>One type per RM/EM/CS state \u2014 rejected: RM is per-participant, so most    such types are ill-defined at the case level.</li> <li>Staged types on every state-bearing class, keyed on any monotonic    milestone \u2014 rejected: proliferates types that add no fields.</li> <li>Field-set-anchored staged types (chosen): a milestone earns a type only    when it changes the guaranteed (non-None) field set; everything else is    modeled as predicates + preconditions.</li> </ol> <p>For the mechanism of the chosen option, two sub-options were weighed and are recorded under \"Pros and Cons\": Pydantic subclasses narrowing fields (recommended) vs. a discriminated union of sibling types.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: field-set-anchored staged types.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#governing-principle","title":"Governing principle","text":"<p>A lifecycle milestone earns a distinct staged type only when it changes the set of guaranteed (required, non-None) fields. A milestone that only changes which actions are permitted \u2014 without changing which fields are present \u2014 belongs in the transition model and precondition specs, not the type hierarchy.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0033-lifecycle-staged-case-types/#what-this-yields","title":"What this yields","text":"<ul> <li><code>VulnerabilityCase</code> staged family (the only staged types): <code>IncomingReport</code> \u2192 <code>Case</code> \u2192 <code>EmbargoedCase</code>.</li> <li><code>IncomingReport</code>: report data, no case assignment (pre-case).</li> <li><code>Case</code>: a case exists \u2014 ADR-0015 creates it at report receipt, so it always     has \u22651 report, the reporter and receiver participants (two parties), and     a seeded <code>case_statuses</code>.</li> <li><code>EmbargoedCase</code>: <code>em_state \u2208 {ACTIVE, REVISE}</code>, so <code>active_embargo</code> is     guaranteed non-None. This is monotonic: EM never returns to     <code>NONE</code>/<code>PROPOSED</code> once <code>ACTIVE</code> (see <code>vultron/core/states/em.py</code>).</li> <li><code>ParticipantStatus</code> and <code>CaseStatus</code>: no subtypes. Each Actor is an isolated process: it owns a DataLayer of core domain objects, and (per the Actor Knowledge Model) its knowledge of the world is bounded strictly by what it has received. No actor can reach into another actor's DataLayer. Wire (AS2) exists solely as the transport by which one actor's core state informs another's \u2014 an AS2 Activity is an envelope carrying a core domain fact across the process boundary, not a domain object in its own right.</p> <p>ADR-0017 established that wire is a projection of core, and ARCH-09-001 requires core models to be as rich as or richer than their wire counterparts. The 29 AS2 protocol Activities (<code>Offer</code>, <code>Invite</code>, <code>Accept</code>, <code>Reject</code>, \u2026) break this: they were built wire-first and were never given a core counterpart. For these types the projection is inverted \u2014 wire is the only representation, and is therefore richer than core.</p> <p>The concrete consequence: when an actor must remember what a message told it (the case id an <code>Invite</code> carried, the recommender an <code>Offer</code> named, the report embedded in a submit <code>Offer</code>, the pending embargo proposal for a case), there is no core object to hold that fact, so core reaches back through the DataLayer and re-reads the stored wire envelope \u2014 <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> inside <code>vultron/core/</code>. Concern #1506 audited these sites. ADR-0034 recognised activity read-back as a boundary violation but explicitly scoped it out and deferred it to a separate concern; this ADR is that concern's decision.</p> <p>The <code>dl.read(activity_id)</code> call in core is a symptom. The root cause is a missing layer of core domain representation for protocol facts. A second, subtler question surfaced during analysis: emitting a reply (e.g. an <code>Accept</code>) requires the full inline verbatim original activity in the reply's <code>object_</code> (the Actor Knowledge Model forbids bare URIs), and activity ids are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values \u2014 so the original envelope cannot be losslessly reconstructed from core state. Does that legitimise reading a stored activity back?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Restore \"wire is a projection of core\" (ADR-0017) and ARCH-09-001: every   domain fact an actor remembers MUST have a home in core.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-03-001 (AS2\u2194domain mapping happens in exactly one place, the   semantic extractor) \u2014 core MUST NOT re-interpret an activity a second time.</li> <li>Honour ARCH-01-002 / DL-05: wire vocabulary types MUST NOT enter core through   the persistence port.</li> <li>Do not regress into cloning each AS2 Activity into a 1:1 core Activity class \u2014   the generic-event-mirroring-AS2 anti-pattern <code>notes/domain-model-separation.md</code>   warns against.</li> <li>Satisfy the Actor Knowledge Model's requirement that replies embed the full   inline original activity, given that activity ids are not regenerable.</li> <li>Keep the migration measurable and regression-proof via the DL-05-004 ratchet.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0035-core-activity-representation-and-envelope-reconstitution/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. That stream travels over a transport with no ordering guarantee, and Vultron may not be the only protocol implementation on the wire, so a replica can receive an entry before its hash-chain predecessor arrives.</p> <p>The original receive path (<code>CheckHashOrRejectOnMismatchNode</code>) treated any entry whose <code>prev_log_hash</code> did not match the local tail as a divergence: it dropped the entry and sent a <code>Reject(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> so the CaseActor would replay the missing prefix. At case closure this stalled a late-joining replica (Vendor2 in the FVV/FVCV demos) indefinitely and <code>wait_for_contiguous_ledger_coverage</code> timed out (issue #1556). How should a replica handle an entry that is valid but arrives before its predecessor?</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Convergence must not depend on <code>Announce</code> delivery order (SYNC-10-004 requires   a contiguous prefix; the transport does not provide ordering).</li> <li>The fix must interoperate with unknown implementations \u2014 we cannot assume the   sender retries, or that any recovery message is delivered in order either.</li> <li>Must preserve the effects-before-persist invariant (SYNC-12-001) and the   DataLayer-presence-means-committed invariant (SYNC-13-001).</li> <li>Bounded memory under a broken or hostile peer that streams far-future entries.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>A. Repair the <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> loop only \u2014 keep dropping out-of-order   entries; make the CaseActor reliably process the participant's Reject and   replay the missing prefix promptly.</li> <li>B. Receiver-side buffering \u2014 hold out-of-order entries locally and apply   them in hash-chain order once their predecessor arrives.</li> <li>C. Both \u2014 buffering plus a hardened replay loop.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: B, receiver-side buffering (which subsumes most of C).</p> <p>Option A alone is insufficient: the replay path re-announces each missing entry as a separate <code>Announce</code>, which travels the same unordered transport and can reorder again \u2014 hitting the very same drop. Repairing replay narrows the race but cannot close it under adversarial reordering. Buffering, by contrast, makes convergence order-independent: any valid entry is retained until the entry that closes its gap arrives, then drained in order.</p> <p>Buffering also makes the existing <code>Reject \u2192 replay</code> recovery order-robust for free, because replayed entries flow through the same (now buffering) receive path. We therefore did not redesign the replay loop; we keep sending the <code>Reject</code> at buffer time purely as the backstop for entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. A companion correctness fix makes <code>SyncActivityAdapter.send_reject_log_entry</code> enqueue against the explicit receiving <code>actor_id</code> (like the announce path) instead of the DataLayer's own scope, so the Reject is delivered correctly even from a shared or differently-scoped DataLayer.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: a late-joining replica converges to a contiguous prefix within a few   seconds of the tail arriving, regardless of <code>Announce</code> order (SYNC-10-004).</li> <li>Good: no new dependence on sender retry behavior \u2014 robust against other   implementations and lossy/reordering transports.</li> <li>Good: the buffer is a non-ledger holding area (SYNC-13-003), so the   \"DataLayer presence \u21d2 committed + effects applied\" invariant is preserved.</li> <li>Neutral: buffered state is in-memory and lost on restart; the SYNC-10 catch-up   gate re-syncs any gap after restart, so no durability is required.</li> <li>Bad: adds a per-actor in-memory structure and a drain step on the receive   path; bounded by a size cap with farthest-ahead eviction (recoverable via the   Reject backstop).</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<ul> <li><code>LedgerGapBuffer</code> unit tests (<code>test/core/models/test_ledger_gap_buffer.py</code>):   O(1) drain-next, multi-hop cascade, per-case isolation, duplicate/fork   handling, size-bound eviction, per-actor registry.</li> <li>Out-of-order regression tests through <code>AnnounceLedgerEntryReceivedUseCase</code>   (<code>test/core/use_cases/received/test_sync.py</code>): fully-reversed delivery,   single-gap click-into-place, multi-gap cascade, shuffled-replay convergence \u2014   each asserting no entry is permanently dropped.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#pros-and-cons-of-the-options","title":"Pros and Cons of the Options","text":""},{"location":"adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries/#a-repair-the-reject-replay-loop-only","title":"A. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Here we describe a notional MPCVD <code>Case</code> object that incorporates the process models and formalisms that define the Vultron Protocol. The object model we describe is intended to provide the necessary core information for an implementation of the formal protocol. The diagram below depicts a UML Class Diagram of the <code>Case</code> model. It is not the minimal possible model required by the Vultron Protocol; for example, strictly speaking, a Participant does not need to attempt to track the state of every other Participant, but it might help to do so. They are used to represent actions that are performed by actors. The ActivityStreams vocabulary defines a number of activities, and we extend these with specific activities that are used in the Vultron AS vocabulary. So far, we have found the ActivityStreams vocabulary to be sufficient for our needs, so our extensions are limited to specifying the types of activities, actors, and objects that are used in the Vultron protocol.</p> <p>A full mapping of Vultron to ActivityStreams is available in the Vultron ActivityStreams Ontology.</p> <p>Design Goals</p> <p>Our goal in each of these activity definitions is to</p> <ul> <li>Avoid creating new activity types when an existing activity type can be used.</li> <li>Avoid creating defined activity types with the same objects and targets to avoid confusion. These include:</p> <ul> <li><code>as:Read</code></li> <li><code>as:View</code></li> <li><code>as:Listen</code></li> </ul> <p>Since most CVD cases are text-centric, we expect that the <code>as:Read</code> activity will be the most commonly used. However, we also expect that the <code>as:View</code> and <code>as:Listen</code> activities could be used in some cases, such as when a case participant views a video or listens to an audio recording.</p> <p>We specifically defined <code>RmReadReport</code> as a subclass of <code>as:Read</code> to indicate that a report has been read. This allows the receiver of a report to acknowledge receipt without indicating anything more than that the report has been read. That leaves <code>RmValidateReport</code> and <code>RmInvalidateReport</code> to indicate a more specific action (accept, reject) on the part of the receiver.</p> <pre><code>flowchart LR\n    subgraph RM:Received\n        a{Accept?}\n        subgraph as:Read\n            RmReadReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Start\n        subgraph as:Offer\n            RmSubmitReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Accepted\n        subgraph as:Accept\n            RmValidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    subgraph RM:Invalid\n        subgraph as:Reject\n            RmInvalidateReport\n        end\n    end\n    a --&gt;|y| RmValidateReport\n    a --&gt;|undecided| RmReadReport\n    a --&gt;|n| RmInvalidateReport\n    RmSubmitReport --&gt; a</code></pre> <p>More Acknowledgements in the Ontology</p> <p>The Vultron AS ontology defines a number of ActivityStreams activities that can serve as the various acknowledgements that are used in the Vultron protocol. These include messages that are specifically <code>as:inReplyTo</code> a message defined as one of the core protocol message types.</p> <p>For example, it is not necessary to send a separate <code>RmReadReport</code> message if the <code>RmValidateReport</code> message is sent as a reply to the <code>RmSubmitReport</code> message. The <code>RmValidateReport</code> message logically indicates that the report has been read in order to have been validated.</p> <p>Like, Dislike and Flag</p> <p>The ActivityStreams vocabulary also includes actions that indicate an opinion  about a message or object, such as <code>as:Like</code>, <code>as:Dislike</code>, and <code>as:Flag</code>. While these may be relevant to implementations of the Vultron protocol, we do not have specific use cases for them at this time.</p>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/acknowledge/#demo","title":"Demo","text":"<p>Try it: <code>vultron-demo acknowledge</code></p> <p>Run this workflow end-to-end with the unified demo CLI:</p> <pre><code>vultron-demo acknowledge\n</code></pre> <p>Or with Docker Compose:</p> <pre><code>DEMO=acknowledge docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm demo\n</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/error/","title":"Error Handling","text":"<p>While the ActivityStreams vocabulary doesn't include any specific error messages, we can use the <code>as:Reject</code> activity to indicate that a message has been rejected for some reason. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>The process to establish an embargo for a case can start in one of two ways:</p> <ul> <li>Any participant can propose an embargo for a case. This is the most common   way to establish an embargo.</li> <li>The case owner can add an embargo to a case without proposing it first. In some circumstances, this might be an   appropriate way to establish an embargo.</li> </ul> <p></p> <p>Embargo Management in Vultron</p> <p>The Vultron protocol contains quite a bit of detail about Embargo Management and how participants are expected to interact with embargoes. Please refer to that section for more information.</p> <p>Why would you add an embargo without asking first?</p> <p>There are a few reasons why you might want to add an embargo to a case without asking first. For example, when the finder is also the case owner and hasn't invited any other participants to join the case yet, the finder can just add an embargo. Then when the finder invites others to join the case, the invited participants can decide whether to accept the embargo or not. This could be an appropriate way to address the concept of Default Embargoes.</p> <pre><code>flowchart TB\n    subgraph as:Invite\n        EmProposeEmbargo\n    end\n    subgraph as:Question\n <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Inviting an actor to a case is a way to add them as a participant in the case. The invitation is sent to the actor as an <code>as:Invite</code> activity. Depending on the actor's response, they may become a participant in the case.</p> <p> </p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Invite Actor to Case\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor O as Case Owner\n    actor A as Actor\n    participant C as Case\n    activate O\n    O -&gt;&gt;+ A: Invite(actor=CaseOwner, object=Actor, target=Case)\n    note over A: Consider invitation\n    alt Accept Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; O: Accept(object=Invite)\n        alt Create CaseParticipant\n        O -&gt;&gt; C: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        else Add CaseParticipant\n        O -&gt;&gt; O: Create(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor))\n        O -&gt;&gt; C: Add(object=CaseParticipant(actor=Actor), target=Case)\n        end\n        note over C: Actor becomes participant in case\n    else Reject Invitation\n        A --&gt;&gt; O: Reject(object=Invite)\n        note over C: Actor is not participant in case\n    end\n    deactivate A\n    deactivate O</code></pre> <p>Invite vs Add?</p> <p>When a case is first created, the Case Owner and any known participants (e.g., the Reporter) should be automatically added to the case. See Initializing a Case for more.</p> <p>However, over the lifespan of a case, there may be other actors that were not already involved at the time the case was created, but who should be invited to participate in the case. We chose to  represent them separately here to acknowledge the difference between creating a new object and adding an existing object to another object, but in an actual implementation it may be acceptable to use either activity for both cases. It seems likely that the general idea should be to use <code>as:Create</code> when creating a new object to  add to another object (as the <code>target</code> of the activity), and <code>as:Add</code> when adding an existing object to another object. </p> <p>That said, our intent is that Vultron be consistent with however ActivityPub does this. An <code>Offer</code> can include a <code>Report</code> object that the sender created immediately before sending. While a <code>Create(Report)</code> technically precedes an <code>Offer(Report)</code>, in practice the receiver usually only observes the <code>Offer</code> because the report was created entirely on the sender's side.</p> <p>In other cases the <code>Report</code> may have been created earlier or by a different actor (for example, a platform or intermediary). When that happens the <code>Create(Report)</code> and <code>Offer(Report)</code> are distinct activities. We show both patterns here to cover both workflows.</p> <p>When would <code>Create(Report)</code> be separate from <code>Offer(Report)</code>?</p> <p>A security researcher files a report with a bug-bounty platform that implements Vultron. Case","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>During the course of coordinating a case, an existing case participant might recognize that another actor should be invited to participate in the case. The following mechanisms provide a way for a case participant to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case.</p> <p> </p> <p>Why Suggest instead of just Invite?</p> <p>The process described here makes an assumption that there is a case owner who is responsible for coordinating the  case. Participants having the case owner role can in principle just directly invite other actors to participate in  the case, and they might not need the suggestion mechanism described here. However, we include this mechanism to account for the possibilities that:</p> <ul> <li>there could be multiple case owners, and they might not all agree on who should be invited to participate in the    case.</li> <li>a non-case-owner participant might want to suggest that another actor be invited to participate in the case</li> </ul> <p>Of these, the latter is the more likely scenario, but the mechanism described here can be used in either case.    </p> <p>Reasons to Invite other Actors</p> <p>There are many reasons why a case participant might want to suggest another actor to participate in a case. The following are some examples:</p> <ul> <li>A finder, having reported to one vendor, might further discover that the vulnerability is actually in a    third-party library, and suggest inviting the library vendor to participate in the case.</li> <li>A vendor might be a participant in (but not the owner of) a case, and wants to suggest that the case owner   invite a sector-specific coordinator to participate in the case to address critical infrastructure concerns.</li> <li>A reporter participant might suggest a technical expert (for example, a member of a protocol working group) to    include in the case.</li> <li>A coordinator might suggest to the case owner that a large deployer be invited to participat in a case to    address concerns about the impact of deploying a fix for a vulnerability on infrastructure and operations.</li> </ul> <p>Below is a sequence diagram showing the process of suggesting an actor for a case. We used a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Suggesting an Actor for a Case (ADR-0026 CaseActor-routed)\n---\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Recommender\n    participant CA as CaseActor\n    actor B as Case Owner\n    actor D as Invitee\n    Note over A: Recognize that Actor should be invited\n    A -&gt;&gt; CA: Offer(object=Actor, target=Case)\n    activate CA\n    Note over CA: Record in ledger, assign default roles\n    CA -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=CaseParticipant{actor,roles}, target=Case, origin=Offer.id)\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Accept(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: AcceptActorRecommendation\n        CA -&gt;&gt;+ D: Invite(CaseStub + embargo + roles)\n        note over D: Respond to invitation (not shown)\n        deactivate D\n    else Reject Suggestion\n        B -&gt;&gt; CA: Reject(object=Offer(CaseParticipant))\n        CA -&gt;&gt; A: RejectActorRecommendation\n    end\n    deactivate B\n    deactivate CA</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/suggest_actor/#recommend-actor","title":"Recommend Actor","text":"<p>A participant recommends another actor to the CaseActor by sending an <code>Offer</code> activity with the <code>object</code> property set to the actor being recommended and the <code>target</code> set to the case. core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Transfer if case ownership was not part of the original Vultron protocol, but it seems like a reasonable extension that could be useful in some cases, such as transferring a case</p> <ul> <li>from a researcher to a vendor</li> <li>from a vendor to an upstream vendor</li> <li>from a vendor to a coordinator</li> <li>from a coordinator to a vendor</li> <li>between coordinators</li> </ul> <p>The presumption here is that the initial creator of a case is its owner. Subsequent to that, the existing owner can offer to transfer ownership to another participant. The new owner can then accept or reject the offer.</p> <p>We use a sequence diagram instead of a flow chart since the process is relatively simple and the sequence diagram is easier to read.</p> <pre><code>sequenceDiagram\n    actor A as Current Case Owner\n    actor B as Potential Case Owner\n    participant C as Case\n    A -&gt;&gt; B: Offer(object=Case)\n    note over B: Consider offer\n    activate B\n    alt Accept Offer\n        B --&gt;&gt; A: Accept(object=Offer)\n        A -&gt;&gt; C: Update(object=Case)\n        note over C: Case has new owner\n    else Reject Offer\n        B --&gt;&gt; A: Reject(object=Offer)\n        note over C: Case ownership unchanged\n    end\n    deactivate B</code></pre>"},{"location":"howto/activitypub/activities/transfer_ownership/#offer-case-ownership-transfer","title":"Offer Case Ownership Transfer","text":"<p>The current owner of a case can offer What exactly is a process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Each Participant in a Case runs one Process. A Process maintains a Composite State \u2014 that's a 3-tuple: (Case State, RM State, EM State).\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"So if a Vendor is in the case, they're one Process?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Exactly. The Vendor runs their own RM state machine, tracks the shared EM state, and maintains their part of the Case State (Vendor Fix Path). Meanwhile, a Coordinator in the same Case is another Process with their own RM state and the same EM state.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"And they coordinate through Message Types?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Yes. When a Vendor transitions their RM from Valid to Accepted, they send an RA (Report Accepted) Message Type. That Activity carries the RA and is transmitted via the wire protocol. The Coordinator receives it and updates their model of the Vendor's RM State.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"But that doesn't change the Coordinator's own RM state?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Correct. The RA message is an announcement \u2014 'I accepted the report.' It doesn't command the receiver to do anything. Only Report Submission (RS) directly changes receiver RM state.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"What about CS Events \u2014 if the Vendor completes a fix, do they have to send a message?\"</p> <p>Formal Spec Expert: \"Not technically. The Vendor internal transitions from Vfd to VFd is a CS Event (F). But per the protocol, they SHOULD announce it by sending a CF (Fix Readiness) message. The Case Status is separate\u2014it shows the collective state across all parties.\"</p> <p>Protocol Designer: \"And when we send an Activity about a State Transition to all participants, we're not telling them to do the transition\u2014we're informing them that we did it?\"</p> <p>Domain Expert: \"Exactly. Most activity in Vultron involves actors exchanging activity messages containing objects.</p> <p>Submitting a Vulnerability Report</p> <p>For example, an actor might create a <code>VulnerabilityReport</code> object and then offer it to another actor, who can then accept, tentatively reject, or  reject the offer.</p> <p>Actors in ActivityPub can be of various types, such as <code>Person</code>, <code>Organization</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Application</code>, <code>Service</code>, etc. Each actor has an inbox and an outbox. The inbox is where the actor receives activities, and the outbox is where the actor sends activities.</p> <p>Actor Inboxes and Outboxes</p> <p>For example, if Alice is a <code>Person</code> actor, she has an inbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/inbox</code> and an outbox at <code>https://example.com/users/alice/outbox</code>. If Bob is another <code>Person</code> actor, he has his own inbox and outbox.</p> <p>When Alice wants to send an activity to Bob, she creates the activity with the <code>to</code> field set to Bob's actor ID (e.g., <code>https://example.com/users/bob</code>) and places it in her outbox. The ActivityPub server then delivers the activity to Bob's inbox. Bob can then process the activity and respond by sending an activity to his outbox, with the <code>to</code> field set to Alice's actor ID. He can also set the <code>inReplyTo</code> field to reference the original activity from Alice to indicate that it is a response. The ActivityPub server handles the delivery of the activity to Alice's inbox,  and the cycle continues.</p> <p>Scope of Vultron's ActivityPub Implementation</p> <p>However, in our Vultron prototype, we are not implementing a full ActivityPub server. Instead, we're initially focusing on the core functionality of actors sending activities directly to each other's inboxes. This simplifies the implementation while still allowing us to demonstrate the core concepts of ActivityPub interactions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#inbox-handler-architecture","title":"Inbox Handler Architecture","text":"<p>Our initial architecture is as follows: An actor has an inbox implemented as a FastAPI endpoint that accepts POST requests containing activity messages. This decouples the raw activity message structure from the higher-level semantics of the Vultron protocol, allowing us to translate raw messages into meaningful semantics that drive application logic.</p> <p>Defining Activity Patterns</p> <p>We might define an activity pattern for submitting a vulnerability report as an <code>Offer</code> activity with an object of type <code>VulnerabilityReport</code>. The handler function is then invoked with the <code>DispatchEvent</code> object as an argument.</p> <p>Example</p> <p>The following is an example of the <code>ActivityDispatcher</code> Protocol that defines   the interface for dispatching activities:</p> <pre><code>class ActivityDispatcher(Protocol):\n    \"\"\"\n    Protocol for dispatching activities to their corresponding handlers based on message semantics.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    def dispatch(self, dispatchable: DispatchEvent) -&gt; None:\n        \"\"\"Dispatches an activity to the appropriate handler based on its semantic type.\"\"\"\n        ...\n</code></pre> <p>On the Modularity of Dispatchers</p> <p>The dispatch function is designed as a Python <code>Protocol</code> to allow for different dispatcher implementations. This provides flexibility in connecting the inbox  handler to specific handler functions for each semantic type. A simple  implementation might use a dictionary mapping from semantic types to handler  functions, while a more complex implementation could involve message queues  or other routing mechanisms.</p> <p>This modularity allows us to easily extend dispatching logic by defining new  <code>ActivityPattern</code>s with corresponding <code>MessageSemantics</code>, then adding new  handler functions to the dispatch mapping. By decoupling routing logic from  handling logic, we maintain clean separation of concerns and facilitate  future protocol extensions.</p>"},{"location":"reference/inbox_handler/#direct-dispatch-implementation","title":"Direct Dispatch Implementation","text":"<p>Our first dispatch function implementation uses a simple direct dispatch approach with a dictionary mapping from <code>MessageSemantics</code> to handler functions. As above, \"\\(\\iff\\)\" indicates the bidirectional equivalence.</p> <p>SSVC Report Public Decision Point Mapped to CS States</p> \\[SSVC(report~public) =  \\begin{cases}     Yes &amp; \\iff q^{cs} \\in \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot P \\cdot\\cdot \\\\     No &amp; \\iff q^{cs} \\in \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot p \\cdot\\cdot \\\\ \\end{cases}\\]"},{"location":"reference/ssvc_crosswalk/#supplier-contacted","title":"Supplier Contacted","text":"<p>If the Supplier (Vendor) has been notified (i.e., there is reason to believe they are at least in the RM Received state, equivalent to the \\(V\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\) CS state subset) the Supplier Contacted value should be Yes, otherwise it should be No.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Contacted Decision Point Mapped to RM States</p> \\[ SSVC(supp.~contacted) =  \\begin{cases}     Yes &amp; \\iff q^{rm}_{Vendor} \\not \\in S \\text{ or } q^{cs}_{Vendor} \\in V\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot \\\\     \\\\     No &amp; \\iff q^{rm}_{Vendor} \\in S \\text{ or } q^{cs}_{Vendor} \\in vfd \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot \\\\ \\end{cases} \\]"},{"location":"reference/ssvc_crosswalk/#report-credibility","title":"Report Credibility","text":"<p>Unlike most of the other SSVC decision points covered here that form a part of a Participant's report prioritization process after report validation, the Report Credibility decision point forms an important step in the Coordinator's validation process. In fact, it is often the only validation step possible when the Coordinator lacks the ability to reproduce a vulnerability whether due to constraints of resources, time, or skill. Thus, a value of Credible can be expected to lead to an RM transition to Valid (\\(q^{rm} \\in R \\xrightarrow{v} V\\)), assuming any additional validation checks also pass. Ampliative means that publication might providing additional information or reach to information that may or may not already be public. From the Coordinator's perspective, if enough Suppliers in a CVD case have communicated their engagement in a case (i.e., enough Vendors are in the RM Accepted state already or are expected to make it there soon from either the Received or Valid states), then the SSVC value would be Active.</p> <p>Vendors in Invalid or Closed can be taken as disengaged, and it might be appropriate to select Unresponsive for the SSVC Engagement decision point.</p> <p>Vendors in either Received or Deferred might be either Active or Unresponsive, depending on the specific report history.</p> <p>This mapping is formalized below and in the figure that follows.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Engagement Decision Point Mapped to RM States</p> \\[ SSVC(supp.~eng.) =  \\begin{cases}     Active &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\} \\\\     \\\\     \\begin{cases}         Active \\\\         Unresponsive     \\end{cases} &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{R,D\\} \\\\     \\\\     Unresponsive &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{I,C,S\\} \\\\ \\end{cases}\\] <pre><code>---\ntitle: \"RM States and SSVC Supplier Engagement\"\n---\ngraph LR\n    subgraph ssvc_se[SSVC Supplier Engagement]\n        Active\n        Unresponsive\n    end\n    subgraph rm_states[RM States]\n        S[Start]\n        R[Received]\n        I[Invalid]\n        V[Valid]\n        D[Deferred]\n        A[Accepted]\n        C[Closed]\n    end\n    A --&gt; Active\n    V --&gt; Active\n    R --&gt; Active\n    D --&gt; Active\n    R--&gt; Unresponsive\n    D --&gt; Unresponsive\n    I --&gt; Unresponsive\n    C --&gt; Unresponsive\n    S --&gt; Unresponsive</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/ssvc_crosswalk/#supplier-involvement","title":"Supplier Involvement","text":"<p>The Supplier Involvement decision point can take on the values Fix-Ready, Cooperative, or Uncooperative/Unresponsive. We begin by noting the equivalence of the Fix-Ready value with the similarly named substate of the CS model.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Involvement Decision Point Mapped to CS States</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     SSVC(supp.~inv.) = Fix~Ready \\iff q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot \\end{aligned}\\] <p>The Vendor RM states map onto these values as formalized below and shown in the figure below.</p> <p>SSVC Supplier Involvement Decision Point Mapped to Vendor RM States</p> \\[\\begin{aligned} SSVC(supp.~inv.) =  \\begin{cases}     \\begin{cases}         Fix~Ready \\\\         Cooperative     \\end{cases} &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in A \\\\     \\\\     Cooperative &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in V \\\\     \\\\     Uncoop./Unresp. &amp; \\text{if } q^{rm} \\in \\{R,I,D,C,S\\} \\\\ \\end{cases} \\end{aligned}\\] <pre><code>---\ntitle: \"RM States and SSVC Supplier Involvement\"\n---\ngraph LR\n    subgraph rm_states[RM States]\n        S[Start]\n        R[Received]\n        I[Invalid]\n        V[Valid]\n        D[Deferred]\n        A[Accepted]\n        C[Closed]\n    end\n\n    subgraph ssvc_si[SSVC Supplier Involvement]\n        fr[Fix-Ready]\n        co[Cooperative]\n        un[Uncooperative/Unresponsive]\n    end\n    A --&gt; fr\n    A --&gt; co\n    V --&gt; co\n    R --&gt; un\n    D --&gt; un\n    I --&gt; un\n    C --&gt; un\n    S --&gt; un</code></pre> <p>Engagement vs. Involvement: What's the Difference?</p> <p>Note the discrepancy between the mappings given for SSVC Supplier Engagement versus those for Supplier Involvement. This distinction is most prominent in the connections from the Received and Deferred RM states in the two figures above. These differences are the result of the relative timing of the two different decisions they support within a CVD case.</p> <p>The decision to Coordinate (i.e., whether the Coordinator should move from RM Valid to RM Accept  (\\(q^{rm} \\in V \\xrightarrow{a} A\\)) occurs early in the Coordinator's RM process. The SSVC Supplier Engagement decision point is an attempt to capture this information. This early in the process, allowances must be made for Vendors who may not have completed their own validation or  prioritization processes.  Hence, the mapping allows Vendors in any valid yet unclosed state (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{R,V,A,D\\}\\)) to be categorized as  Active for this decision point.</p> <p>On the other hand, the decision to Publish\u2014a choice that falls entirely within the Coordinator's RM Accepted  state\u2014occurs later, at which time, more is known about each Vendor's level of involvement in the case to that point.  By the time the publication decision is made, the Vendor(s) have had ample opportunity to engage in the CVD process. They might already have a Fix-Ready (\\(q^{cs} \\in VF \\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\cdot\\)), or they might be working toward it (i.e., SSVC Cooperative). However, if the Coordinator has reached the point where they are making a publication decision, and the Vendor has  yet to actively engage in the case for whatever reason\u2014as indicated by their failure to reach the RM Accepted state or demonstrate progress toward it by at least getting to RM Valid  (\\(q^{rm} \\in \\{A,V\\}\\))\u2014then they can be categorized as Uncooperative/Unresponsive.</p> <p>SSVC Decision Points and Anticipated Transitions</p> <p>Other SSVC decision points may be informative about which transitions to expect in a case. Two examples apply here:</p> <ol> <li>Supplier Engagement acts to gauge the likelihood of the F transitions. Coordination becomes more necessary the lower that likelihood is.</li> <li>Utility (the usefulness of the exploit to the adversary) acts to gauge the likelihood of the A transition.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"reference/terms/","title":"Terms and Definitions","text":"<p>Throughout this documentation, we refer to CVD Roles from the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure:</p> <p>Finder</p> <p>The individual or organization that identifies the vulnerability</p> <p>Reporter</p> <p>The individual or organization that notifies the vendor of the vulnerability</p> <p>Vendor (Supplier)</p> <p>The individual or organization that created or maintains the vulnerable product</p> <p>The Vendor role is synonymous with the Supplier role as it appears in SSVC Version 2 and above.</p> <p>Deployer (User)</p> <p>The individual or organization that must deploy a patch or take other remediation action</p> <p>The Deployer role is synonymous with the User role in ISO/IEC 29147:2018 and ISO/IEC 30111:2019, while the other roles are named consistent with those standards.</p> <p>Coordinator</p> <p>An individual or organization that facilitates the coordinated response process</p> <p>We also add a new role in this documentation, which we expect to incorporate into a future version of the CVD Guide:</p> <p>Exploit Publisher</p> <p>An individual or organization that publishes exploits</p> <p>Exploit Publishers might be the same as Finders, Reporters, Coordinators, or Vendors, but this is not guaranteed. For example, Vendors that produce tools for Cybersecurity Red Teams might play a combination of roles: Finder, Reporter, Vendor, Coordinator, and/or Exploit Publisher.</p> <p>Finally, we have a few additional terms to define:</p> <p>CVD Case (Case)</p> <p>The unit of work for the overall CVD process for a specific vulnerability spanning the individual CVD Case Participants and their respective processes</p> <p>CVD Case Participant (Participant)</p> <p>Finder, Vendor, Coordinator, Deployer, etc., as defined above</p> <p>Vulnerability Report (Report)</p> <p>The unit of work for an individual Case Participant's Report Management (RM) process</p> <p>A diagram showing the relationship between CVD Cases, Participants, and Reports can be found in Case Object.</p>"},{"location":"reference/two-actor-demo-protocol/","title":"Two-Actor Demo \u2014 Protocol Reference","text":"<p>This document is a technical reference for the two-actor (Finder + Vendor) CVD demo. Implementations of the Vultron Protocol are expected to have their own versioning schemes.</p> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev3641+g6903494aa</p> <p>Vultron Protocol versions follow Calendar Versioning (CalVer) using the format <code>YYYY.M.Patch</code>, where:</p> <ul> <li> <p><code>YYYY</code> is the four-digit year of the most recent non-patch release.</p> </li> <li> <p><code>M</code> is the month of the most recent non-patch release,     with no zero padding (e.g., <code>1</code>, <code>2</code>, <code>3</code>, ..., <code>12</code>).</p> </li> <li> <p><code>Patch</code> is the patch number for that release.     For the first (or only) release in a given month, the patch number     starts at <code>0</code> and is normally omitted, so <code>2024.4.0</code> and <code>2024.4</code>     denote the same version.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Version increments work as follows:</p> <ul> <li> <p>Significant releases use the current year and month, with the patch     number starting at <code>0</code> (normally omitted).     Example: the first significant release in April 2024 is <code>2024.4</code>.</p> </li> <li> <p>Patch releases increment the patch number from the most recent     non-patch release, even if the patch is published in a later month or year.     Example: the third small update to <code>2024.4</code> is <code>2024.4.3</code>, even if it     is released in May 2024 or later.</p> </li> </ul> <p>Because we are still in the early stages of the project, no backward compatibility commitments are made or implied at this time. We anticipate this will change as the protocol matures.</p>"},{"location":"reference/case_states/","title":"Index","text":""},{"location":"reference/case_states/#case-states","title":"Case This design allows us to separate the core domain logic from the infrastructure and external interfaces, making the system more modular, testable, and adaptable to different use cases and environments.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Overview\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nadapters1[Driving Adapters]\nadapters2[Driven Adapters]\nports1[Driving Ports]\nports2[Driven Ports]\ncore{{Core Domain Logic}}\nadapters1 --o ports1\nports1 --o core\ncore --o ports2\nports2 --o adapters2</code></pre> <p>In this architecture:</p> <ul> <li>The Driving Adapters implement the driving ports using specific   technologies (e.g., FastAPI endpoints, CLI commands, etc.) and translate   external inputs into calls to the core domain logic.</li> <li>The Driving Ports define the interfaces through which external actors   (e.g., finders, vendors, coordinators) can interact with the core domain logic. These are the entry points for commands and queries that drive the system's behavior.</li> <li>The Core Domain Logic contains the business rules, policies, and behavior trees that govern how the system operates. It is completely agnostic to how it is accessed or what technologies are used to implement the interfaces.</li> <li>The Driven Ports define the interfaces through which the core domain   logic can interact with external systems (e.g., databases, message queues,   external APIs). These are the exit points for the core to perform actions   that have side effects or require external resources.</li> <li>The Driven Adapters implement the driven ports using specific technologies   (e.g., MongoDB for database access, Celery for task queues, etc.)   and   translate calls from the core domain logic into interactions with external   systems.</li> </ul> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Hexagonal Architecture Details\n---\nflowchart LR\n\nsubgraph driving_adapters [Driving Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    api[API Endpoints]\n    cli[CLI Commands]\n    mcp[MCP Tools]\nend\nsubgraph driving_ports [Driving Ports]\n    direction LR\n    use_cases[Use Cases]\n    commands[Commands]\nend\nsubgraph core [Core Domain Logic]\n    direction LR\n    domain_models[Domain Models]\n    services[Domain Services]\n    behavior_trees[Behavior Trees]\nend\nsubgraph driven_ports [Driven Ports]\n    direction LR\n    database[Database Access]\n    message_queue[Message Queue]\n    external_apis[External APIs]\nend\nsubgraph driven_adapters [Driven Adapters]\n    direction LR\n    mongo[MongoDB Adapter]\n    celery[Celery Adapter]\n    vince[VINCE Adapter]\nend\n\ndriving_adapters --&gt; driving_ports\ndriving_ports --&gt; core\ncore --&gt; driven_ports\ndriven_ports --&gt; driven_adapters</code></pre>"},{"location":"reference/code/api/actor_inbox_handler/","title":"Actor Inbox Handler","text":"<p>The Actor Inbox Handler is the hub that processes incoming activities. <code>as_Object</code></p> <p>https://www.w3.org/TR/activitystreams-vocabulary/#dfn-activity An Activity is a subtype of Object that describes some form of action that may happen, is currently happening, or has already happened. The Activity type itself serves as an abstract base type for all types of activities. It is important to note that an Activity is not a representation of a currently executing process, but rather a statement about that process. For example, a person walking down the street is not an Activity unless they are posting a picture of themselves walking down the street.       Bases: <code>as_Base</code></p> <p>A Link is an indirect, qualified reference to a resource identified by a URL. The fundamental model for links is established by [RFC5988]. Many of the properties defined by the Activity Vocabulary allow values that are either instances of Object or a Link. When a Link is used, it establishes a qualified relation connecting the subject to the resource identified by the href property. Brand and Zafiropulo defined a protocol as follows.</p> <p>Protocol Formally Defined</p> <p>A protocol with \\(N\\) processes is a quadruple:</p> \\[ protocol =      \\Big \\langle          { \\langle S_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},          { \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1},         { \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle}^N_{i,j=1},         { succ }     \\Big \\rangle\\] <p>Where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(N\\) is a positive integer representing the number of processes.</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle S_i \\rangle_{i=1}^N\\) are \\(N\\) disjoint finite sets (\\(S_i\\) represents the set of states of process \\(i\\)).</p> </li> <li> <p>Each \\(o_i\\) is an element of \\(S_i\\) representing the initial state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\). \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\),</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(succ\\) is a partial function mapping for each \\(i\\) and \\(j\\), $\\(S_i \\times M_{ij} \\rightarrow S_i \\textrm{ and } S_i \\times M_{ji} \\rightarrow S_i\\)$ \\(succ(s,x)\\) is the state entered after a process transmits or receives message \\(x\\) in state \\(s\\). It is a transmission if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ij}\\) and a reception if \\(x\\) is from \\(M_{ji}\\).</p> </li> </ul> <p>Global State Formally Defined</p> <p>The global state of a protocol given by the above is a pair \\(\\langle S, C \\rangle\\), where</p> <ul> <li> <p>\\(S\\) is an \\(N\\)-tuple of states \\(\\langle s_1,\\dots,s_N \\rangle\\) with each \\(s_i\\) representing the current state of process \\(i\\).</p> </li> <li> <p>\\(C\\) is an \\(N^2\\)-tuple \\(\\langle c_{1,1},\\dots, c_{1,N}, c_{2,1}, \\dots \\dots, c_{N,N} \\rangle\\), where each \\(c_{i,j}\\) is a sequence of messages from \\(M_{i,j}\\). The message sequence \\(c_{i,j}\\) represents the contents of the channel from process \\(i\\) to \\(j\\). (Note that \\(c_{i,j}\\) is empty when \\(i = j\\) since processes are presumed to not communicate with themselves.)</p> </li> </ul> <p>We detail each of these below or in subsequent pages:</p> <ul> <li>\\(N\\) below</li> <li>\\({ \\langle S_i \\rangle}^N_{i=1}\\), and \\({ \\langle o_i \\rangle }^N_{i=1}\\) in States,</li> <li>\\({ \\langle M_{i,j} \\rangle }^N_{i,j=1}\\) in Message Types,</li> <li>\\({ succ }\\) in Transition Functions</li> </ul>"},{"location":"reference/formal_protocol/#number-of-processes","title":"Number of Processes","text":"<p>The processes we are concerned with represent the different Participants in their roles (Finder, Vendor, Coordinator, Deployer, and Other). Revisiting the definitions from the Formal Protocol Introduction:</p> <p>Formalism</p> <p>\\(\\langle M_{ij} \\rangle_{i,j=1}^N\\) are \\(N^2\\) disjoint finite sets with \\(M_{ii}\\) empty for all \\(i\\): \\(M_{ij}\\) represents the messages that can be sent from process \\(i\\) to process \\(j\\).</p> <p>The message types in the Vultron Protocol arise primarily from the following principle taken directly from the CVD Guide:</p> <p>Avoid Surprise</p> <p>As with most situations in which multiple parties are engaged in a potentially stressful and contentious negotiation, surprise tends to increase the risk of a negative outcome. The importance of clearly communicating expectations across all parties involved in a CVD process cannot be overemphasized. If we expect cooperation between all parties and stakeholders, we should do our best to match their expectations of being \"in the loop\" and minimize their surprise. Publicly disclosing a vulnerability without coordinating first can result in panic and an aversion to future cooperation from Vendors and Finders alike. CVD promotes continued cooperation and increases the likelihood that future vulnerabilities will also be addressed and remedied.</p> <p>Now we condense that principle into the following protocol recommendation:</p> <p>Participants whose state changes in the RM, EM, or CVD State Models SHOULD send a message to other Participants for each transition.</p> <p>If you are looking for a one-sentence summary of the entire Vultron Protocol, that was it.</p> <p>State Transitions</p> <ul> <li>RM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{rm} = \\{ r,v,a,i,d,c\\}\\)</li> <li>EM state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{em} = \\{ p,a,r,t\\}\\)</li> <li>CVD state transitions \\(\\Sigma^{cs} = \\{\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A}\\}\\)</li> </ul> <p>As a reminder, those transitions are shown at right.</p> <p>We will address the specific circumstances when each message should be emitted in Transitions, but first we need to introduce the message types this recommendation implies. In this section, we seek to fill that gap.  We begin by deriving a model of all possible CVD histories from first  principles, organizing those histories into a partial ordering based on a  set of desired criteria. We then compute a baseline expectation for the  frequency of each desired criteria and propose a new set of performance  indicators to measure the efficacy of CVD practices based on the  differentiation of skill and luck in observation data. As a proof of concept, we apply these indicators to a variety of longitudinal observations of CVD practice and find evidence of significant skill to be prevalent. We  conclude with reflections on how this model and its accompanying performance indicators could be used by various stakeholders (vendors, system owners, coordinators, and governments) to interpret the quality of their CVD practices.</p> <p>This section is derived from the following paper: A State-Based Model for Multi-Party Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (MPCVD) by Allen Householder and The need for MPCVD arises due to the inherent nature of the software supply chain CERT Guide to CVD. A vulnerability that affects a low-level component (such as a library or operating system API) can require fixes from both the originating vendor and any vendor whose products incorporate the affected component. Alternatively, vulnerabilities are sometimes found in protocol specifications or other design-time issues where multiple vendors may have each implemented their own components based on a vulnerable design.</p>"},{"location":"reference/measuring_cvd/benchmarking_mpcvd/#state-tracking-in-mpcvd","title":"State Tracking in MPCVD","text":"<p>Applying our state-based model to MPCVD requires a forking approach to the state tracking.</p> <p>MPCVD Case State Tracking</p> <p>At the time of discovery, the vulnerability is in state \\(vfdpxa\\). Known only to its finder, the vulnerability can be described by that singular state.</p> <p>As it becomes clear that the vulnerability affects multiple vendors' products, both finder/reporters and coordinators might begin to track the state of each individual vendor as a separate instance of the model. For example, if 3 vendors are known to be affected, but only 1 has been notified, the case might be considered to be in a superposition of states \\(\\{Vfdpxa,vfdpxa,vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>Each vendor, in turn, might then ascertain whether they are able to produce fixes for all their available products at once, or if those fixes will be staggered over time. In either case, the vendor might track the case as a superposition of states for each affected product dependent on its fix readiness status. For example, a vendor might have four products affected, with two in the fix-ready state and two fixes still in progress. Should they opt for transparency into their internal process, they might communicate their status as the superposition of \\(\\{VFdpxa,VFdpxa,Vfdpxa,Vfdpxa\\}\\). Alternatively, they might choose to only share the lowest state across their products, which in this example would be \\(\\{Vfdpxa\\}\\).</p> <p>The above example implies a need to expand our notation.</p> <p>MPCVD Cases have Participant-Specific States</p> <p>In the MPCVD case, we need to think of each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\) as a set of states \\(q_M\\):</p> \\[ q_M \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ q_1,q_2,\\dots,q_n \\} \\] <p>where \\(q_i\\) represents the state \\(q\\) for the \\(i\\)th affected vendor and/or product. For example, \\(\\{ {Vfdpxa}_1, {vfdpxa}_2 \\}\\) would represent the state in which vendor 1 has been notified but vendor 2 has not. Very often, vendor notification occurs as new products and vendors are identified as affected in the course of analyzing a vulnerability report. Further discussion of measuring MPCVD skill can be found below.</p> <p>Reducing Dimensionality of MPCVD Cases is a good thing</p> <p>For now, we posit that the goal of a good MPCVD process is to reduce the dimensionality of a given MPCVD case as much as is possible (i.e., to the 5 dimensions of a single vendor CVD case we have presented above). Experience shows that a full dimension reduction is unlikely in most cases, but that does not detract from the value of having the goal.</p> <p>Reducing Complexity within a Vendor Organization</p> <p>Vendors may be able to reduce their internal tracking dimensionality---which may be driven by things like component reuse across products or product lines---through in-house coordination of fix development processes. Within an individual vendor organization, PSIRTs are a common organizational structure to address this internal coordination process.</p> <ul> <li>The FIRST PSIRT Services Framework provides guidance regarding vendors' internal processes for coordinating vulnerability response.</li> <li>Additional guidance can be found in ISO/IEC 30111:2019.</li> </ul> <p>Regardless, the cross-vendor dimension is largely the result of component reuse across vendors, for example through the inclusion of third party libraries or OEM SDKs. Visibility of cross-vendor component reuse remains an unsolved problem, although efforts such as the Software Bill of Materials are promising in this regard. Thus, dimensionality reduction can be achieved through both improved transparency of the software supply chain and the process of coordination toward synchronized state transitions, especially for \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), if not for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) as well.</p> <p>As a result of the dimensionality problem, coordinators and other parties to an MPCVD case need to decide how to apply disclosure policy rules in cases where different products or vendors occupy different case states with potentially contradictory recommended actions. For example, when four out of five vendors involved in a case have reached \\(VFdpxa\\) and are ready to publish, but the fifth is still in \\(Vfdpxa\\). Essentially this can be expected to take the form of a weighting function that acts on a vector of case states, and outputs a set of recommended actions derived from those states.</p> <p>One possible function would be to apply a simple voting heuristic such as waiting for a simple majority of vendors to reach a state before taking action as that state recommends. In our 4/5 \\(VFdpxa\\) example, the coordinating parties would simply behave as if the case were in that state for all.</p> <p>Another function could be to weight vendors and products by some other factor, such as size of the installed user base, or even based on a risk analysis of societal costs associated with potential actions. Here we acknowledge that our example is under-specified: does the fifth vendor (the one in \\(Vfdpxa\\)) represent a sizable fraction of the total user base? Or does it concentrate the highest risk use cases for the software? Challenges in efficiently assessing consistent answers to these questions are easy to imagine. The status quo for MPCVD appears consistent with defaulting to simple majority in the absence of additional information, with consideration given to the distribution of both users and risk on a case-by-case basis. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>Does CVD as observed in the wild demonstrate skillful behavior?</p> <p>In order to answer this question, we need a way to measure skillful behavior in CVD. This section defines a method for measuring skill in CVD.</p> <p>The measurement method makes use of all the modeling tools and baselines established thus far: a comprehensive set of possible histories \\(\\mathcal{H}\\), a partial order over them in terms of the presence of desired event precedence \\((\\mathcal{H},\\leq_{\\mathbb{D}})\\), and the a priori expected frequency of each desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\).</p> <p>If we expected to be able to observe all events in all CVD cases, we could be assured of having complete histories and could be done here.
