Now, we want to measure the degree to which a CVD practice is skillful in achieving those desiderata. In a world of pure skill, one would expect that a player could achieve all 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) consistently. That is, a maximally skillful player could consistently achieve the specific ordering \\(h=(\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{F},\\mathbf{D},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A})\\) with probability \\(p_{skill} = 1\\).</p> <p>Factors that could affect the observed frequency of a desideratum</p> <p>There are many reasons why we might expect our observations to differ from the expected frequencies we established  in Reasoning Over Possible Histories. Adversaries might be rare, or conversely very well equipped. Vendors might be very good at releasing fixes faster  than adversaries can discover vulnerabilities and develop exploits for them. System owners might be diligent at applying patches. (We did say might, didn't we?) Regardless, for now we will lump all of those possible explanations into a single attribute called \"skill.\"</p> <p>Thus, we construct the following model: for each of our preferred orderings \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), we model their occurrence due to luck using the binomial distribution with parameter \\(p_{luck} = f_d\\) taken from the event frequency table in Reasoning Over Possible Histories, reproduced below for convenience:</p> <p>Expected Frequency of \\({row} \\prec {col}\\) when events are chosen uniformly from possible transitions in each state</p> \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) \\(\\mathbf{V}\\) 0 1 1 0.333 0.667 0.750 \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) 0 0 1 0.111 0.333 0.375 \\(\\mathbf{D}\\) 0 0 0 0.037 0.167 0.187 \\(\\mathbf{P}\\) 0.667 0.889 0.963 0 0.500 0.667 \\(\\mathbf{X}\\) 0.333 0.667 0.833 0.500 0 0.500 \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) 0.250 0.625 0.812 0.333 0.500 0 <p>Recall that the mean of a binomial distribution is simply the probability of success \\(p\\), and that the mean of a weighted mixture of two binomial distributions is simply the weighted mixture of the individual means. Therefore our model adds a parameter \\(\\alpha_d\\) to represent the weighting between our success rates arising from skill \\(p_{skill}\\) and luck \\(p_{luck}\\). Because there are 12 desiderata \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\), each \\(d\\) will have its own observations and corresponding value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) for each history \\(h_a\\).</p> <p>Modeling Skill and Luck in Observations</p> <p>We model the observed frequency of desiderata \\(d\\) as a weighted mixture of the success rates due to skill and luck:</p> \\[ f_d^{obs} = \\alpha_d \\cdot p_{skill} + (1 - \\alpha_d) \\cdot p_{luck} \\] <p>Where \\(f_d^{obs}\\) is the observed frequency of successes for desiderata \\(d\\). When we refer to the \\(\\alpha_d\\) coefficient for a specific \\(d\\) we will use the specific ordering as the subscript, for example: \\(\\alpha_{\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}}\\).</p> \\[ \\alpha_\\mathbb{D} \\stackrel{\\mathsf{def}}{=}\\{ \\alpha_d : d \\in \\mathbb{D} \\} \\] <p>The concept embodied by \\(f_d\\) is founded on the idea that if attackers and defenders are in a state of equilibrium, the frequency of observed outcomes (i.e., how often each desiderata \\(d\\) and history \\(h\\) actually occurs) will appear consistent with those predicted by chance. So another way of interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) is as a measure of the degree to which a set of observed histories is out of equilibrium.</p> <p>Interpreting \\(\\alpha_d\\) Behavior</p> <p>The following are a few comments on how \\(\\alpha_d\\) behaves. Note that \\(\\alpha_d &lt; 0\\) when \\(0 \\leq f_d^{obs} &lt; f_d\\) and \\(0 \\leq \\alpha_d \\leq 1\\) when \\(f_d \\leq f_d^{obs} \\leq 1\\). The implication is that a negative value for \\(\\alpha_d\\) indicates that our observed outcomes are actually worse than those predicted by pure luck. In other words, we can only infer positive skill when the observations are higher (\\(f_d^{obs} &gt; f_d\\)). That makes intuitive sense: if you are likely to win purely by chance, then you have to attribute most of your wins to luck rather than skill. From the event frequency table above, the largest value for any \\(d \\in \\mathbb{D}\\) is \\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}=0.75\\), implying that even if a vendor knows about 7 out of 10 vulnerabilities before attacks occur (\\(f_{\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{A}}^{obs} = 0.7\\)), they are still not doing better than random.</p> <p>On the other hand, when \\(f_d\\) is small it is easier to infer skill should we observe anything better than \\(f_d\\). While we could just estimate the error in our observations using the binomial's variance \\(np(1-p)\\), because of boundary conditions at 0 and 1 we should not assume symmetric error. An extensive discussion of uncertainty in the binomial distribution is given in <sup>1</sup>.</p> <p>However, for our purpose the Beta distribution lends itself to this problem nicely. The Beta distribution is specified by two parameters \\((a,b)\\). It is common to interpret \\(a\\) as the number of successes and \\(b\\) as the number of failures in a set of observations of Bernoulli trials to estimate the mean of the binomial distribution from which the observations are drawn. For any given mean, the width of the Beta distribution narrows as the total number of trials increases.</p> <p>We use this interpretation to estimate a 95% credible interval for \\(f_d^{obs}\\) using a Beta distribution with parameters \\(a = S_d^{obs}\\) as successes and \\(b = T - S_d^{obs}\\) representing the number of failures using the <code>scipy.stats.beta.interval</code> function in Python. This gives us an upper and lower estimate for \\(f_d^{obs}\\), which we multiply by \\(T\\) to get upper and lower estimates of \\(S_d^{obs}\\) as in Observed Success Frequency above.</p> <ol> <li> <p>Lawrence D Brown, T Tony Cai, and Anirban DasGupta. Although within the page we might provide guidance in terms of SHOULD, MUST, etc., the content here is not normative.</p> <p>To begin to differentiate skill from chance in the next few sections, we need a model of what the CVD world would look like without any skill. We cannot derive this model by observation. Even when CVD was first practiced in the 1980s, some people may have had social, technical, or organizational skills that transferred to better CVD. We follow the principle of indifference as stated below.</p> <p></p> <p>Benjamin Eva in Principles of Indifference</p> <p>Let \\(X = \\{x_1,x_2,...,x_n\\}\\) be a partition of the set \\(W\\) of possible worlds into \\(n\\) mutually exclusive and jointly exhaustive possibilities. In the absence of any relevant evidence pertaining to which cell of the partition is the true one, a rational agent should assign an equal initial credence of \\(n\\) to each cell.</p> <p>While the principle of indifference is rather strong, it is inherently difficult to reason about absolutely skill-less CVD when the work of CVD is, by its nature, a skilled job. Given the set of states and allowable transitions between them, we can apply the principle of indifference to define a baseline against which measurement can be meaningful.</p>"},{"location":"reference/measuring_cvd/random_walk/#estimating-state-transition-probabilities","title":"Estimating State Transition Probabilities","text":"<p>Our assumption is that transitions are equally probable, not that states or histories are. The events \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\) trigger state transitions according to \\(\\delta\\) and the histories \\(h \\in \\mathcal{H}\\) are paths (traces) through the states. This meets the definition above because each \\(\\sigma \\in \\Sigma\\) is unique (mutually exclusive) and \\(\\delta\\) defines an exhaustive set of valid \\(\\sigma\\) at each state \\(q \\in \\mathcal{Q}\\).</p> <p>Initial State Probabilities</p> <p>For example, because causality requires \\(\\mathbf{V} \\prec \\mathbf{F}\\) and \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{D}\\), only four of the six events in \\(\\Sigma\\) are possible at the beginning of each history at \\(q_0=vfdpxa\\): \\(\\{\\mathbf{V},\\mathbf{P},\\mathbf{X},\\mathbf{A}\\}\\). The PageRank algorithm provides a probability estimate for each state based on a Markov random walk of the directed graph of states. PageRank assumes each available transition is equally probable, consistent with our model. To avoid becoming stuck in dead ends, PageRank adds a teleport feature by which walks can, with a small probability, randomly jump to another node in the graph.</p> <p>Before proceeding, we need to make a small modification of our state digraph. Without modification, the PageRank algorithm will tend to be biased toward later states because the only way to reach the earlier states is for the algorithm to teleport there. Teleportation chooses states uniformly, so for example there is only a \\(1/32\\) chance of our actual start state (\\(q_0={vfdpxa}\\)) ever being chosen. Therefore, to ensure that the early states in our process are fairly represented we add a single link from VFDPXA to vfdpxa, representing a model reset whenever the end state is reached. This modification allows PageRank traversals to wrap around naturally and reach the early states in the random walk process without needing to rely on teleportation. With our modification in place, we are ready to compute the PageRank of each node in the graph. Results are shown in the preceding table.</p>"},{"location":"reference/measuring_cvd/reasoning_over_histories/","title":"Reasoning over Possible Histories","text":"<p>This page is not normative</p> <p>This page is not considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol as proposed in the main documentation. Each stage has distinct error semantics and MUST NOT be conflated.Conflating stages (e.g., treating a transport timeout as a recipient rejection) leads to incorrect retry logic and protocol-state divergence. The three-stage model is the foundation for correct at-least-once delivery. Source: <code>notes/architecture-adapters.md</code>. <code>ARCH-19-002</code> MUST Emission (stage 1) MUST be idempotent with respect to the outbox: writing the same activity ID twice MUST NOT create a duplicate outbox entry. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-003</code> MUST Transport delivery (stage 2) MUST be retried on transient network failures. The retry mechanism MUST be implemented in the outbox worker, not in the use-case or handler. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-004</code> MUST NOT A transport delivery failure (stage 2 error) MUST NOT be interpreted as recipient rejection (stage 3 semantics). Delivery failure means the activity did not reach the recipient; it carries no information about whether the recipient would accept or reject the activity. Refines: ARCH-19-001 <code>ARCH-19-005</code> MUST The outbox worker MUST record the delivery outcome (success, transient failure, or permanent failure) in the per-actor process log (Python <code>logging</code>) at the level prescribed in <code>specs/structured-logging.yaml</code>. Delivery outcomes MUST NOT be written to the canonical case ledger; the case ledger is exclusively for CaseActor-authored protocol-significant assertions (ADR-0019).ADR-0019 establishes strict separation: the canonical case ledger contains only CaseActor-authored protocol assertions; per-actor transport observability goes to the process log. Delivery outcomes (whether a network call succeeded) are operational diagnostics, not protocol-significant assertions. A node whose automation potential is High but whose inputs arrive from an external source or whose outputs affect an external system is a Retriever, Sentinel, Evaluator, Composer, or Actuator \u2014 not ProtocolInternal \u2014 regardless of how automated the implementation may be.Automation potential and call-out point shape are orthogonal dimensions. Automation potential describes whether the call-out point logic can be executed without human involvement; shape describes the structural pattern of the seam (what flows in, what flows out, and in what direction). A Retriever backed by a REST API is still a Retriever; the automation just means the Retriever implementation does not require human action. Conflating the two dimensions caused the FUZZ-08a misclassification tracked in issue #1188, where ~38 nodes with High automation potential were incorrectly assigned ProtocolInternal shape, causing downstream work (FUZZ-08a-bis, FUZZ-08d through FUZZ-08g) to build wrong seams. The five canonical shapes are: Sentinel, Evaluator, Retriever, Composer, and Actuator (added in issue #1239). Nodes that invoke external systems to cause side effects without producing a content artifact MUST be classified as Actuator, not Composer. Implements: BT-16-005 \u2014 BT-16-005 defines automation potential categories; BT-18-005 clarifies that those categories govern the automation-potential field only and have no bearing on call-out point shape assignment. <code>BT-18-006</code> MUST A node that queries an external system synchronously and returns only a binary (SUCCESS/FAILURE) result MUST be classified as a Retriever, not a Sentinel. A boolean is the simplest possible structured fact; the defining criterion for Retriever shape is the synchronous on-demand query pattern, not the richness of the returned data. Such a binary-result Retriever has an empty blackboard output-key set: the structured fact is expressed as the BT return value (SUCCESS/FAILURE), not as a blackboard write. BT-18-001 through BT-18-003 apply: the empty output-key set MUST be declared in the node docstring. A Sentinel, by contrast, monitors a condition continuously (or is triggered by an external event) and calls a trigger endpoint when the condition becomes true; the flow direction is Sentinel \u2192 trigger endpoint \u2192 protocol, not protocol \u2192 query \u2192 external system.The Sentinel vs. Retriever ambiguity surfaced with nodes such as MitigationDeployed, MitigationAvailable, and HaveExploit (issue #1240). These nodes appear sentinel-like because they return only SUCCESS/FAILURE, but they are invoked synchronously by the BT (on-demand) and query an external system to determine the current status. That is the Retriever pattern. A true Sentinel is not invoked by the BT; it runs independently and calls a trigger endpoint when a condition fires. Capturing the fact once at extraction time removes the need for core to reach back through the wire envelope. This does NOT mean cloning each AS2 Activity into a 1:1 core Activity class; model only the domain fact each message conveys, in domain vocabulary, capturing only what handlers use. Decided in ADR-0035. * Implements: ARCH-03-001 <code>DL-06-003</code> MUST When an inbound protocol message references a prior message (e.g. an Accept answering an Invite, a counter-offer answering an Offer), core MUST correlate them through a core-entity relationship (e.g. \"the pending embargo proposal for this case\", \"the invitation for this actor\"), NOT by re-reading the referenced wire activity from the DataLayer. *Correlation is a domain relationship between core facts. Recovering it by re-reading the referenced activity reintroduces the DL-06-001 violation and depends on the wire envelope surviving as a semantic record. When the prior message was first received it MUST have created or updated the core entity that the later message now correlates to. Decided in ADR-0035. * <code>DL-06-004</code> MUST Reconstituting the verbatim original activity for an outbound reply's inline <code>object_</code> / <code>in_reply_to</code> field (as the Actor Knowledge Model requires) MAY read a stored activity payload back, but this retrieval MUST be owned by the wire/adapter layer and treat the stored activity as an opaque envelope; core code MUST NOT read the activity to interpret its meaning. Such a wire/adapter-owned envelope seam is NOT counted as a core boundary violation under DL-05-004. *Activity IDs are non-regenerable random <code>urn:uuid:</code> values and the Actor Knowledge Model requires a reply to embed the full inline original activity, so verbatim reconstitution cannot be produced by re-projecting core state \u2014 the original envelope (with its original id) must be retained and read back. Confining that read to a wire/adapter seam that never interprets the payload keeps semantic authority in core while satisfying transport needs. <code>CaseLedgerEntry</code> <code>payloadSnapshot</code> is the existing precedent for opaque, write-only activity retention. Decided in ADR-0035. * Refines: DL-05-004 <code>DL-06-005</code> MUST As each core semantic read is migrated off activity read-back (per DL-06-001 through DL-06-003), the corresponding AS2 Activity type MUST be removed from the DL-05-004 ratchet exemption set. The exemption set MUST reach zero once all core semantic activity reads are migrated; the only remaining sanctioned activity reads are the wire/adapter envelope-reconstitution seam of DL-06-004. *Ties the migration to an enforceable, monotonically shrinking ratchet so progress is measurable and regressions are blocked. Dropping such an entry and relying on a reject/replay round-trip does not converge under adversarial reordering, because replay re-announces entries individually over the same unordered transport (they can reorder and be dropped again). These requirements make replica convergence independent of delivery order by holding forward-gap entries in a non-ledger buffer and draining them in hash-chain order once the entry that closes the gap is committed. Rationale: ADR-0037 (docs/adr/0037-buffer-out-of-order-ledger-entries.md).</p> ID Priority Requirement Related <code>SYNC-14-001</code> MUST When a participant receives a valid Announce(CaseLedgerEntry) whose prev_log_hash does not match its current chain tail but whose log_index is strictly greater than tail_index + 1 (a forward gap), the participant MUST NOT permanently discard the entry; it MUST retain the entry in a holding area pending arrival of its predecessor.The hash chain makes indefinite retention safe: a held entry is applied only when an entry whose entry_hash equals the held entry's prev_log_hash is committed, so a fork/rewrite cannot masquerade as the predecessor. <code>SYNC-14-002</code> MUST A forward-gap entry that is buffered MUST still trigger resynchronization (SYNC-08-005) \u2014 the participant MUST send Reject(CaseLedgerEntry) carrying its last accepted hash so the CaseActor replays entries that are genuinely lost (never delivered) rather than merely reordered. <code>SYNC-14-003</code> MUST After a participant commits a CaseLedgerEntry, it MUST drain the holding area: for each newly committed tail, it MUST locate the buffered entry (if any) whose prev_log_hash equals the new tail's entry_hash, apply that entry, and repeat, cascading until no buffered entry extends the current tail. <code>SYNC-14-004</code> MUST Draining a buffered entry MUST apply the entry's domain effects before persisting it (SYNC-12-001) and MUST NOT re-apply effects for an entry already present in the local ledger (SYNC-12-003); the drain path MUST be the same apply-then-persist path used for in-order delivery. In the Voltron animated series, a team of protectors joins forces to defend the universe from their adversaries. Their defensive mission requires a combination of independent defenders coordinating their efforts to achieve their goals. Like Voltron, our Vultron Protocol comprises a combination of humans and the technical processes and mechanisms that empower them. Together, those humans, processes, and mechanisms must function both individually and in coordination and cooperation with others to protect information systems and the people who depend on them from exploitation by adversaries.</p> <p>Both usages are relevant to this effort. First, insofar as we seek to scale the MPCVD process through the use of automation and software-augmented human processes, we wish to propose a formal technical protocol that can serve as the basis of such technical tools. The Formal Protocol section of this documentation addresses this first definition in specific detail after explicating its component parts and their interactions in Report Management, Embargo Management, Case State, and Model Interactions.</p> <p>Second, recognizing that MPCVD is primarily a coordination process among human Participants with the goal of remediating extant vulnerabilities in deployed information systems, a protocol must not only address the technical formalities of communicating code but also extend to the expected behaviors of the human Participants that rely on it. Syntactic interoperability, in the form of message formats and the like, is the focus of our ongoing effort.</p> <p>Addressing semantic interoperability first is a deliberate choice. If we were to go in the reverse order, we might wind up with systems that exchange data quickly and accurately yet still fail to accomplish the mutually beneficial outcomes that MPCVD sets out to achieve. Carney et al. illustrate the importance of semantic interoperability in their 2005 report Some Current Approaches to Interoperability:</p> <p>Carney et al. on semantic interoperability</p> <p>There is a limited number of ways that agreements on meaning can be achieved. In the context of design-time interoperability, semantic agreements are reached in the same manner as interface agreements between the constituent systems... However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new system can join, ad-hoc, some other group of systems. The new system must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other systems, and those other systems must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>In this excerpt, replace the word \"system\" with the concept of a \"CVD Case Participant,\" and the need for semantic interoperability as a means of achieving coordination in MPCVD becomes clear:</p> <p>Paraphrasing Carney et al. in the context of CVD</p> <p>[...] However, in the context of run-time interoperability, the situation is more complex, since there is need for some manner of universal agreement, so that a new CVD Participant can join, ad-hoc, some other group of CVD Participants [in a CVD Case]. The new CVD Case Participant must be able to usefully share data and meaning with those other CVD Case Participants, and those other Participants must be able to share data and meaning from an unfamiliar newcomer.</p> <p>Elsewhere in the same report, Carney et al. write,</p> <p>Carney et al. on the necessity of trust in interoperability</p> <p>In the hoped-for context of unbounded systems of systems, trust in the actions and capabilities provided by interoperating parties is essential. Each party to an interaction must have, develop, or perceive a sense of whether the actions of interoperating parties can be trusted. This sense of trust is not Boolean (e.g., parties can be trusted to varying degrees), is context dependent (Party A can be trusted in a particular context but not in another), and is time sensitive (Party A can be trusted for a certain period). Further, the absence of trust-----distrust-----is less dangerous than misplaced trust: it is better to know that you cannot trust a particular party than to misplace trust in a party</p> <p>The protocol we propose is intended to promote trust between MPCVD Participants both within an individual case as well as over time and across cases.</p>"},{"location":"topics/background/interoperability/#objectives","title":"Objectives","text":"<p>The objectives of this documentation are as follows:</p> <ol> <li> <p>Provide a set of common primitives to serve as an ontological     foundation for CVD process definitions across     organizations.</p> </li> <li> <p>Construct abstract workflows that support the inter-organizational     coordination and synchronization required for the     CVD process to     be successful.</p> </li> <li> <p>From those primitives and workflows, identify a set of message types     needed for the CVD process to function.</p> </li> <li> <p>Provide high-level requirements for the semantic content of those     message types.</p> </li> <li> <p>Explore options for the syntactic representation of those message     types.</p> </li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/","title":"Modeling an MPCVD AI Using Behavior Trees","text":"<p>Normative requirements for the behaviors described here</p> <p>The machine-readable behavioral conformance requirements underlying the trees in this section are located in the Protocol Specifications:</p> <ul> <li>RMB \u2014 Report Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>EMB \u2014 Embargo Management Behavioral Requirements</li> <li>CSB \u2014 CVD Case State Behavioral Requirements</li> </ul> <p>Each page in this section lists the relevant spec group IDs in its Requirements section. The behavior tree diagrams illustrate one conformant implementation; implementations are not required to use behavior trees.</p> <p>With the formal definition of the Vultron Protocol behind us, we now turn our attention to reflect on one of many possible paths toward implementation. We find that Behavior Trees have a number of desirable properties when it comes to automating the kinds of complex behaviors our protocol demands.</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees</p> <p>For more about Behavior Trees, see </p> <ul> <li>Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction</li> <li>A behavior language for story-based believable agents</li> <li>GDC 2005 Proceeding: Handling Complexity in the Halo 2 AI</li> <li>Increasing Modularity of UAV Control Systems using Computer Game Behavior Trees</li> <li>An integrated system for autonomous robotics manipulation</li> </ul> <p>Behavior Trees are a way of designing and programming hierarchical behaviors. They originated in the computer gaming industry to develop realistic AIs to control NPCs in games. More recently, Behavior Trees have been used in robotics to create adaptive behaviors using autonomous AI agents. Behavior Trees offer a high potential for automating complex tasks. Agent processes can be modeled as sets of behaviors (pre-conditions, actions, and post-conditions) and the logic that joins them. Behavior Trees offer a way to organize and describe agent behaviors in a straightforward, understandable way.</p> <p>In this section, we use Behavior Trees as a method for describing MPCVD Participant activities and their interactions with the formal protocol. These behaviors map approximately to the activities described in the CVD Guide (e.g., validate report, prioritize report, create fix, publish report, publish fix, deploy fix).</p> <p>If Behavior Trees were merely a notational convention, they would already have been useful enough to include here to structure the high-level business logic of the Vultron Protocol. But they also offer a way to prototype software agents that reflect the activities of CVD Participants. Because Behavior Trees are inherently hierarchical, they are composable. Both conditions and actions can be composed into small task-oriented behaviors, which can, in turn, be composed to represent more complex agent behaviors. As a result, independent agents using Behavior Trees can be composed into multi-agent behaviors that achieve goals.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/#a-brief-introduction-to-behavior-tree-notation","title":"A Brief Introduction to Behavior Tree Notation","text":"<p>Behavior Trees consist of a hierarchy of nodes represented as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). A Behavior Tree execution always begins at the root node, and execution is passed along the tree by ticking each child node according to the logic built into the tree. When ticked, each node does its job and returns one of three statuses: Success, Failure, or Running. A full introduction to Behavior Trees can be found in Colledanchise and \u00d6gren's book Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction.</p> <p>Behavior Tree Node Types</p> Node Type Shape or Symbol Description Root any control flow type has no parent nodes, has one or more child nodes, and can be of any of the control-flow types. Condition rounded oval does not change the state of the world, has no child nodes, and returns only Success or Failure. Task rectangle has no child nodes; performs a task, which might change the state of the world; and returns Success, Failure, or Running. Sequence \u2192 ticks each child node, returning the last Success or the first Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Fallback ? ticks each child node, returning the first Success or the last Failure, or Running if a child returns Running. Loop \u21ba repeatedly ticks child nodes until an exit condition is met. Parallel \u21c9 ticks all child nodes simultaneously, and returns Success when \\(m\\) of \\(n\\) children have returned Success. <p>A basic Behavior Tree is shown below. When a tree is presented in the vertical orientation, each node's children should be read left to right. In the example below, we see two motifs that come up through the remainder of this section. On the left side is a Fallback node (\\(\\boxed{?}\\)), which short-circuits to Success when the \\(postcondition\\) is already met. Otherwise, some activity will occur in \\(task_a\\) and, assuming that it succeeds, the \\(postcondition\\) is set. As a result, the fallback node ensures that Success means that the \\(postcondition\\) is met.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree\n---\nflowchart TD\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>On the right side is a sequence (\\(\\boxed{\\rightarrow}\\)) that hinges on a \\(precondition\\) being met prior to some set of actions being taken. Assuming the \\(precondition\\) is met, \\(task_b\\) fires and, assuming it succeeds execution, proceeds to another fallback node. This fallback node represents a set of tasks in which one only needs to succeed for the fallback to return Success. If \\(task_c\\) succeeds, then \\(task_d\\) does not run.</p> <p>Behavior Trees can sometimes be wider than they are tall, so we sometimes display them in a horizontal orientation to save space. The semantics remain the same, but each node's children should be read top-to-bottom rather than left-to-right. The same tree as above is shown below in horizontal form.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Basic Behavior Tree (horizontal)\n---\nflowchart LR\n    root[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l[?]\n    root --&gt; l\n    r[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    root --&gt; r\n    l0([postcondition])\n    l --&gt; l0\n    l1[\"&amp;rarr;\"]\n    l --&gt; l1\n    l10[task_a]\n    l1 --&gt; l10\n    l11[set postcondition]\n    l1 --&gt; l11\n    r0([precondition])\n    r --&gt; r0\n    r1[task_b]\n    r --&gt; r1\n    r2[?]\n    r --&gt; r2\n    r20[task_c]\n    r2 --&gt; r20\n    r21[task_d]\n    r2 --&gt; r21</code></pre> <p>Behavior Trees are composable\u2014that is, a task node in one tree can be replaced with a more refined Behavior Tree in another. We leverage this feature throughout the remainder of this chapter to describe an agent model for an MPCVD Participant as a set of nested Behavior Trees that reflect the protocol described in the previous chapters.</p>"},{"location":"topics/behavior_logic/acquire_exploit_bt/","title":"Acquire Exploit Behavior","text":"<p>Some Vendors or other CVD Participants might require a proof-of-concept exploit to accompany an incoming report for it to pass their validation checks. Other approaches remain possible---for example, employing a heuristic to avoid catastrophic outcomes for all, then applying a weighted sum over the impact to the remaining users. Embargoes are a common feature of CVD, and the model gives us a way of formally specifying the conditions under which initiating or maintaining an embargo may or may not be appropriate. Disclosure policies specify commitments by coordinating parties to ensure the occurrence of certain state transitions within a specific period of time. While the model presented here does not directly address timing choices, we can point out some ways to relate the model to those choices. Specifically, we intend to demonstrate how disclosure policy SLEs can be stated as rules triggered within subsets of states or by particular transitions between subsets of states in \\(\\mathcal{Q}\\).</p> <p>SLEs and Publication Timing</p> <p>For example, a finder, reporter, or coordinator might commit to publishing information about a vulnerability 30 days after vendor notification. This translates to starting a timer at \\({v} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{V}} {V}\\) and ensuring \\({Vp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VP}\\) when the timer expires. Notice that the prospect of \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP}\\) is often used to motivate vendors to ensure a reasonable SLE to produce fixes (\\({Vf} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VF}\\))  (See for example Optimal Policy for Software Vulnerability Disclosure by Arora, Telang, and Xu).</p> <p>SLEs and Fix Readiness Timing</p> <p>Similarly, a vendor might commit to providing public fixes within 5 business days of report receipt. In that case, the SLE timer would start at \\({vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{V}} {Vfp}\\) and and end at one of two transitions: First, the \"normal\" situation in which the vendor creates a fix and makes it public along with the vulnerability (\\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}\\), i.e., \\({VFp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VFP}\\)). Second, a \"zero day\" situation in which events outside the vendor's control cause the \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP}\\) transition to occur prior to the fix being ready (\\({VfP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VFP}\\)), i.e, \\(\\mathbf{P} \\prec \\mathbf{F}\\). Likewise, the \\({Vfp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {VfP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {VFP}\\) path might also occur when a vendor has set their embargo timer too aggressively for their development process to keep up.</p> <p>It is therefore in the vendor's interest to tune their SLE to reduce the likelihood for unexpected public awareness (\\(\\mathbf{P}\\)) while providing sufficient time for \\(\\mathbf{F}\\) to occur, optimizing to achieve \\(\\mathbf{F} \\prec \\mathbf{P}\\) in a substantial fraction of cases. As future work, measurement of both the incidence and timing of embargo failures through observation of \\(\\mathbf{P}\\), \\(\\mathbf{X}\\), and \\(\\mathbf{A}\\) originating from \\(\\mathcal{Q}_{E}\\) could give insight into appropriate vendor SLEs for fix readiness (\\(\\mathbf{F}\\)).</p> <p>SLEs and Fix Deployment Timing</p> <p>Service providers and VM practitioners might similarly describe their SLEs in terms of timing between states. Such policies will likely take the form of commitments to limit the time spent in \\({FdP}\\). When the vendor has already produced a patch, the clock starts at \\({Fdp} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{P}} {FdP}\\), whereas if the vulnerability becomes public prior to patch the clock starts at \\({fdP} \\xrightarrow{\\mathbf{F}} {FdP}\\). It may be possible to resolve some apparent policy conflicts by delaying notifications to some vendors to ensure that all embargo end timers expire simultaneously. We informally refer to this as the Thanksgiving Dinner problem, due to its similarity to the familiar annual holiday meal in which a number of dishes with varying preparation times are expected to be delivered to the table simultaneously, each at its appropriate temperature and doneness. For example, when one party has a \"minimum 90 days to publish\" policy and another has a \"maximum 5 days to publish\" policy, the resolution could be to notify the first vendor 85 days before notifying the second. Such a model of graduated disclosure could work well for cases where notifications are automated and vendor dependencies are small or where coordinating parties' policies can be resolved as compatible. Technology such as Theorem Provers and Solvers seem likely to be suited to this sort of problem.</p> <p>However, when formal policies are incompatible, the failure to resolve them automatically becomes an opportunity for human intervention as the exception handler of last resort. Of potential concern here are MPCVD cases in which a vendor with a long policy timer is dependent on one with a short policy timer to provide fixes. The serial nature of the dependency creates the potential for a compatibility conflict. For example, this can happen when an OS kernel provider's disclosure policy specifies a shorter embargo timer than the policies of device manufacturers whose products depend on that OS kernel. Protocol. This is a normative section of the documentation.</p> <p>Here we describe the basic primitives necessary for the CVD Embargo Management (EM) process.</p> <p>For our purposes, an embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time relative to the report at hand. Once an embargo has expired, there is no further restriction on publishing information about the vulnerability.</p> <p>Reminder</p> <p>Exploits are information about vulnerabilities too.</p> <p>CVD case Participants must be able to propose, accept, and reject embargo timing proposals according to their individual needs. Additionally, Participants may want to attempt to gain agreement that enables specific details about a vulnerability to be shared with other Participants or made public. Such content considerations are outside the scope of this proposal. We focus our discussion on the when of an embargo, not the what.</p> <p>Embargo Definition</p> <p>An embargo is an informal agreement among peer CVD case Participants to refrain from publishing information about a vulnerability until some future point in time.</p> <p>Unlike the RM model, in which each Participant has their own instance of the RM DFA, EM states are a global property of a CVD case.</p> <p>A CVD case SHALL NOT have more than one active embargo at a time.</p> <p>(We define the term active below.)</p> <p>Even in an MPCVD case having a vertical supply chain\u2014in which Vendors must wait on their upstream suppliers to produce fixes before they can take action on their own, as in the figure below\u2014our intent is that the embargo period terminates when as many Vendors as possible have been given an adequate opportunity to produce a fix.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: A Vertical Supply Chain\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    v1: Originating&lt;br/&gt;Vendor\n    v2: Vendor 2\n    v3: Vendor 3\n    v4: Vendor 4\n    v5: Vendor 5\n    v6: Vendor 6\n\n    v1 --&gt; v2\n    v1 --&gt; v3\n    v2 --&gt; v4\n    v3 --&gt; v5\n    v2 --&gt; v5\n    v5 --&gt; v6</code></pre> <p></p> <p>CVD Embargoes Are Not NDAs</p> <p>CVD embargoes are not Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). An NDA (also known as a Confidentiality agreement) is a legally binding contract between parties, often accompanied by a reward for compliance and/or some penalty in the event of unauthorized disclosure. NDAs do, on occasion, have a place in CVD processes, but the relatively rapid pace and scale of most MPCVD embargoes makes per-case NDAs prohibitively difficult. As a result, we are intentionally setting aside NDA negotiation as beyond the scope of this proposal.</p> <p>On the surface, many bug bounty programs may appear to fall outside our scope because they are often structured as  NDAs in which compliance is rewarded. This is intentional, and it results directly from the asymmetry mentioned in Negotiating Embargoes The Receiver is faced with a choice to either accept the Reporter's proposal and attempt to extend it or to reject the proposal and end up with no embargo at all. Therefore, if we take the stance that for a vulnerability with no fix available, any embargo is better than no embargo, it should be obvious that it is in the Receiver's interest to accept even a short proposed embargo before immediately working to revise it.</p> <p>The alternative is impractical because the Reporter is not obligated to provide the report to the Receiver at all. In the scenario where a Reporter proposes a short embargo and the Receiver rejects it because it is not long enough, the Reporter might choose to exit the negotiation entirely and publish whenever they choose without ever providing the report to the Receiver. That is not to say that we recommend this sort of behavior from Reporters. In fact, we specifically recommend the opposite in Negotiating Embargoes. Rather, it once more acknowledges the time-dependent informational asymmetry inherent to the CVD process.</p> <p>A Logical Argument for Accepting the Shortest Proposed Embargo</p> <p>Perhaps the above reasoning comes across as too Machiavellian for some readers. Here is a different perspective: Say a Reporter proposes an embargo of n days, while the Vendor would prefer m days. If n and m are given in units of days, we can look at them as a series of individual agreements, each of 1 day in length. We will represent each Participant as a vector representing that Participant's willingness to perpetuate the embargo on each day. Embargo willingness will be represented as a 1 if the Participant is willing to commit to keeping the embargo on that day, and a 0 if they are not. For simplicity's sake, we assume that each Participant is willing to maintain the embargo up to a certain point, and then their willingness goes away. In other words, each vector will be a series of zero or more _1_s followed by zero or more _0_s. For example, \\([1,1,1,1,0,0,0]\\) represents a Participant's willingness to engage in a 4-day embargo.</p> <p>For our two Participants, let \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\) be zero-indexed vectors of length \\(max(n,m)\\).</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     |\\mathbf{x}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\\\     |\\mathbf{y}| &amp;= max(n,m) \\end{aligned}\\] <p>The elements of each vector represent each respective Participant's willingness for the embargo to persist on each consecutive day.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{x} =          \\begin{bmatrix} x_i :         x_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; n \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise} \\\\         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)         \\end{bmatrix} \\\\     \\mathbf{y} =         \\begin{bmatrix} y_i :          y_i =          \\begin{cases}             1 &amp;\\text{if }i &lt; m \\\\             0 &amp;\\text{otherwise}         \\end{cases}         &amp; \\text{ for } 0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Note that we have constructed these vectors so that each vector's scalar sum is just the length of embargo they prefer.</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{x}) &amp;= n \\\\     \\Sigma(\\mathbf{y}) &amp;= m  \\end{aligned}\\] <p>Now we can define an agreement vector \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as the pairwise logical AND (\\(\\wedge\\)) of elements from \\(\\mathbf{x}_ and _\\mathbf{y}\\):</p> \\[\\begin{aligned}     \\mathbf{z} =      \\begin{bmatrix} z_i :          z_i = x_i \\land y_i         &amp; \\text{for }0 \\leq i &lt; max(n,m)     \\end{bmatrix} \\end{aligned}\\] <p>For example, if one party prefers an embargo of length \\(n=4\\) days while another prefers one of length \\(m=7\\) days, we can apply \\(\\mathbf{x}\\), \\(\\mathbf{y}\\), and \\(\\mathbf{z}\\) as follows:</p> \\[\\begin{split}     \\mathbf{x} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0] \\\\     \\wedge~\\mathbf{y} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,1,1,1] \\\\     \\hline     \\mathbf{z} &amp;= [1,1,1,1,0,0,0]     \\end{split}\\] <p>From this, we can see that the scalar sum of the agreement vector---and therefore the longest embargo acceptable to both parties---is simply the lesser of n and m:</p> \\[\\Sigma ( \\mathbf{z} ) = min(n,m)\\] <p>As an example:</p> <p>The Shortest Proposed Embargo Wins</p> <p>If a Reporter proposes a 90-day embargo, but the Vendor prefers a 30-day embargo, we can think of this as a series of 1-day agreements in which both parties agree to the first 30 days of the embargo and disagree beyond that. By accepting the shorter 30-day embargo, the Reporter now has 30 days to continue negotiations with the Vendor to extend the embargo. Even if those continued negotiations fail, both parties get at least the 30-day embargo period they agreed on in the first place. This should be preferable to both parties versus the alternative of no embargo at all were they to simply reject the shorter proposal.</p> <pre><code>---\ntitle: Embargo Agreement in a Nutshell\n---\nstateDiagram-v2\n    direction LR\n    dots: ...\n    state Agreement {\n        direction LR\n        [*] --&gt; 1\n        1 --&gt; 2\n        2 --&gt; dots\n        dots --&gt; 30\n        negotiate: negotiate extension\n        [*] --&gt; negotiate\n        negotiate --&gt; 30\n    }\n    30 --&gt; 31\n    state Disagreement {\n        dots2: ...\n        31 --&gt; dots2\n        dots2 --&gt; 90\n    }</code></pre> <p>Typically it is the Reporter who desires a shorter embargo than the Vendor. We chose our example to demonstrate that this analysis works between any two parties, regardless of which party wants the shorter embargo.</p> <p>Resolving Multiple Proposals at Once</p> <p>On our way to making this principle explicit, we immediately came across a second scenario worth a brief diversion: What to do when multiple revisions are up for negotiation simultaneously? Based on the idea of extending the above to an efficient pairwise evaluation of multiple proposals, we suggest the following heuristic:</p> <ol> <li>Sort the proposals in order from earliest to latest according to their expiration date.</li> <li>Set the current candidate to the earliest proposal.</li> <li>Loop over each remaining (later) proposal, evaluating it against the current candidate.</li> <li>If the newly evaluated proposal is accepted, it becomes the current candidate and the loop repeats.</li> <li>Otherwise, the loop exits at the first rejected proposal.</li> <li>The current candidate (i.e., the latest accepted proposal) becomes the new Active embargo.</li> <li>If the earliest proposed revision is rejected---implying that none of the later ones would be acceptable either---then the existing Active embargo remains intact.</li> </ol>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/defaults/#resolving-proposals-and-revisions","title":"Resolving Proposals and Revisions","text":"<p>Summarizing the principles just laid out as rules</p> <p>When two or more embargo proposals are open (i.e., none have yet been accepted) and \\(q^{em} \\in P\\), Participants SHOULD accept the shortest one and propose the remainder as revisions.</p> <p>When two or more embargo revisions are open (i.e., an embargo is active yet none of the proposals have been decided) and \\(q^{em} \\in R\\), Participants SHOULD accept or reject them individually, in earliest to latest expiration order.</p>"},{"location":"topics/process_models/em/early_termination/","title":"Early Termination","text":"<p>This page is normative</p> <p>This page is considered a core part of the Vultron Protocol. Built on CERT/CC's decades of experience coordinating global software vulnerability response, Vultron aims to serve as a lingua franca for sharing CVD case coordination data across independent organizations, tools, and policies. It targets security researchers, vulnerability coordinators, tool builders, and anyone seeking interoperability in the CVD ecosystem.</p> <p>Work in progress</p> <p>Vultron is a collection of ideas, models, code, and work in progress, and is not yet ready for production use. We are currently working on the documentation of the Vultron CVD Protocol. Our focus so far is on</p> <ul> <li>Explanation, which describes the   protocol in detail</li> <li>How-to Guides, which provides guidance for   potential implementations of Vultron</li> <li>Reference, which provides the formal   protocol specification</li> </ul> <p>Current Version</p> <p>The current version of the Vultron Protocol is</p> <p>2024.4.4.dev3641+g6903494aa</p>"},{"location":"#so-what-is-vultron","title":"So what is Vultron?","text":"<p>Vultron is:</p> <ul> <li>A set of high-level processes representing the steps involved in coordinated   vulnerability disclosure</li> <li>A formal protocol describing the interactions of those processes</li> <li>A set of behavior logic that can be implemented as either procedures for humans   to follow or (in many cases) code that can perform actions in response to state   changes in a case with minimal human input</li> <li>A minimal data model for what information is necessary to track participant   status and the overall case status through the course of handling a CVD case</li> </ul> <p>The above were all initially described in the Designing Vultron: A Protocol for Multi-Party Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (MPCVD) report. In this repository, we are taking the first steps towards implementing the protocol and behavior logic described in that report. The current work focuses on mapping the formal protocol onto the syntax and semantics of the ActivityPub protocol.</p>"},{"location":"#what-is-vultron-not","title":"What is Vultron not?","text":"<p>Vultron is not a drop-in replacement for any particular</p> <ul> <li>tracking system\u2014e.g.,   Bugzilla,   Jira</li> <li>CVD or threat coordination tool\u2014e.g.,   VINCE,   MISP</li> <li>Vulnerability disclosure program\u2014e.g.,   DC3 VDP</li> <li>Vulnerability disclosure platform or service\u2014e.g.,   HackerOne,   Bugcrowd,   Synack</li> </ul> <p>Instead, it is our hope that Vultron could serve as a lingua franca for the exchange of vulnerability case coordination information between those systems and services.</p> <p>Vultron is not a vulnerability prioritization tool, although it is intended to be compatible with common prioritization schemes like SSVC and CVSS.</p> <p>Vultron is not intended to be a product; rather, it is meant to be a feature set that can be implemented in a variety of CVD-related products and services to enable interoperability between them.</p>"},{"location":"#how-this-documentation-is-organized","title":"How this documentation is organized","text":"<p>We are in the process of documenting the Vultron CVD Protocol as we work towards a prototype implementation. Therefore, our position is that end-to-end encryption would be better implemented as a layer on top of the ActivityPub protocol, rather than as a specific feature of the Vultron Protocol. From what we can tell, the topic has come up before in the ActivityPub community, but there is no standardized solution yet. We're currently focused on developing the Vultron Protocol, but we realize that encryption may be a requirement for widespread adoption, so we're keeping an eye on the topic.</p> <p>Some relevant links include:</p> <ul> <li>A November 2022 blog   post Towards End-to-End Encryption for Direct Messages in the Fediverse</li> <li>Issue #225 on the W3C ActivityPub Github repo talks about the   need for encrypted content, but it seems to have been closed without a solution in 2017.</li> <li>However, a much more       recent April 2023 comment       mentions:       &gt; If we restrict to direct message (with a single recipient) one may just encrypt the message (Note) payload using       the       public key of the recipient. We're using the expanded concept of an Any Decision Record (ADR) to capture any decision that is important to the project, not just architectural decisions. We use Markdown Any Decision Records (MADR) to document our architectural decisions.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#when-to-write-an-adr","title":"When to write an ADR","text":"<p>The primary signal for an ADR is evaluated alternatives: if you considered more than one option and rejected at least one, document the decision. The record preserves context for future maintainers who might otherwise re-open a settled question.</p> <p>Concretely, write an ADR when:</p> <ul> <li>You adopted a structural or architectural approach over one or more   alternatives (e.g., hexagonal architecture over layered, SQLModel over   TinyDB).</li> <li>You made a one-time process or tooling decision with lasting project-wide   impact (e.g., CalVer over SemVer, pinning CI action SHAs).</li> <li>A decision will be hard or costly to reverse, so the rationale should be   preserved explicitly.</li> </ul> <p>ADR vs. spec: an ADR records why a choice was made; a spec entry records what the system must do going forward. When a significant decision also generates recurring testable requirements, create both \u2014 see <code>notes/specs-vs-adrs.md</code> for the full delineation guidelines and worked examples.</p> <p>You do not need an ADR for:</p> <ul> <li>Uncontested conventions with no real alternatives (write a spec entry   instead).</li> <li>Small tactical choices where the rationale is obvious from the code.</li> </ul> <p>If you're unsure, err on the side of writing one \u2014 a brief ADR is better than losing context.</p>"},{"location":"adr/#how-to-write-an-adr","title":"How to write an ADR","text":"<p>For new ADRs, please use adr-template.md as basis. implemented as ActivityPub actors with inboxes and outboxes. Inbound messages are ActivityStreams objects, typically Activities that include domain-specific objects (e.g., Vulnerability Reports).</p> <p>Early prototypes implemented inbound message handling using a layered routing model:</p> <ul> <li>Inbox handler</li> <li>Activity-type handler</li> <li>Object-type handler</li> <li>Downstream \u201cwork\u201d execution</li> </ul> <p>This approach introduced several problems:</p> <ul> <li>Loss of semantic cohesion: separating activity handling from object handling discarded context required to determine correct behavior; downstream workers had to reconstruct state already known at receipt time.</li> <li>Poor alignment with existing behavior logic: Vultron already defines message types as (Activity Type, Object Type) tuples, with corresponding behavior trees defined in the protocol simulator. The routing model obscured this mapping.</li> <li>Tight coupling of protocol handling and execution: the inbox handler effectively controlled execution flow, making asynchronous or distributed execution difficult.</li> <li>Deployment inflexibility: the design did not cleanly support both local development (\u201cgit clone + docker-compose up\u201d) and integration into environments with job queues or workers.</li> </ul> <p>These issues indicated a missing architectural boundary between protocol handling and behavior execution.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Preserve semantic context when invoking behavior</li> <li>Align runtime execution with existing message-type semantics</li> <li>Support both simple local deployments and scalable asynchronous architectures</li> <li>Improve testability and separation of concerns</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Keep layered routing inside the inbox handler (current approach)</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: \"Introduce a Behavior Dispatcher abstraction between inbox handling and behavior execution.\"</p> <p>Justification:</p> <ul> <li>Restores a clear execution boundary that preserves semantics determined at receipt time.</li> <li>Keeps behavior trees message-type-specific and implementation-agnostic with respect to invocation mechanics.</li> <li>Enables multiple implementations (in-process direct invocation or queued/asynchronous invocation), supporting both local development and distributed deployments.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good:</li> <li>Removes redundant activity/object routing layers</li> <li>Preserves semantic context at behavior invocation time</li> <li>Aligns runtime execution with existing Vultron message-type semantics</li> <li>Enables both synchronous and asynchronous execution models</li> <li>Supports both local development and scalable deployments</li> <li>Improves testability by isolating behavior trees</li> <li>Bad / Tradeoffs:</li> <li>Introduces an additional abstraction layer</li> <li>Requires explicit dispatcher interface definition and implementations</li> <li>Asynchronous implementations require explicit failure and retry semantics</li> <li>Persistence ordering (write-on-receipt vs behavior-owned writes) must be chosen deliberately</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0007-use-behavior-dispatcher/#validation","title":"Validation","text":"<ul> <li>Code and API reviews of dispatcher interface and implementations</li> <li>Unit and integration ActivityStreams 2.0 (AS2) structural types leaked into domain logic; semantic extraction was scattered across multiple files; handler functions instantiated the persistence layer directly; and the root <code>vultron/</code> package mixed domain enums with wire-format enums. An architectural review (<code>archived_notes/architecture-review.md</code>) catalogued twelve violations of the intended separation of concerns, ranging in severity from minor to critical. A clear architecture decision was needed to guide remediation and prevent the same violations from re-accumulating.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Wire format replaceability: AS2 is the current wire format because its   vocabulary matches Vultron's domain vocabulary. That match must not collapse   the boundary between wire concerns and domain concerns.  If AS2 is replaced   or extended, the change must be absorbable in the wire layer alone.</li> <li>Testability: Core domain logic should be testable with plain domain   objects, without constructing AS2 activities or making HTTP requests.</li> <li>Single extraction seam: The mapping from AS2 vocabulary to domain   semantics must live in exactly one place so that future wire format changes   have a single point of entry.</li> <li>Dependency injection over direct instantiation: Driven adapters   (persistence, delivery) must be injectable to support testing and alternate   backends.</li> <li>Alignment with existing clean points: Several existing patterns are   already architecturally sound (the <code>DataLayer</code> Protocol, <code>DispatchEvent</code>   wrapper, <code>MessageSemantics</code> enum vocabulary, FastAPI 202 + BackgroundTasks)   and should be preserved.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0009-hexagonal-architecture/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Continue organic layering \u2014 Impose light conventions without a formal   architecture pattern. requires every object to have an <code>id</code> field. The <code>generate_new_id()</code> utility in <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/base/utils.py</code> currently returns a bare UUID-4 string (e.g., <code>2196cbb2-fb6f-407c-b473-1ed8ae806578</code>) as the default <code>as_id</code> for new objects. The AS2 specification and the Vultron object-IDs spec (<code>specs/object-ids.yaml</code> OID-01-001) require that <code>id</code> values be full URI identifiers. Bare UUIDs are not valid AS2 identifiers and will cause interoperability problems once federation is implemented.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0010-standardize-object-ids/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>AS2 compliance: ActivityStreams 2.0 requires <code>id</code> to be an absolute   IRI. Bare UUIDs cannot be resolved across systems.</li> <li>Blackboard key safety: py_trees blackboard keys derived from full-URI   IDs must not use the raw URI (which contains slashes). Using the last path   segment or UUID suffix as the key avoids hierarchical key-parsing issues   (OID-03-001).</li> <li>DataLayer compatibility: The DataLayer uses <code>as_id</code> as the primary   lookup key. lifecycle phases with a pivot at <code>RM.VALID</code>:</p> <ul> <li>Report phase (START \u2192 RECEIVED \u2192 INVALID/VALID): Currently tracked in a   transient in-memory <code>STATUS</code> dict The pivot point \u2014 when a report transitions to <code>RM.VALID</code> and a case is created \u2014 is implemented ad hoc with no formal transition from the report-phase record to the case-phase record. New participant status records are seeded with <code>rm_state=RM.START</code> rather than carrying forward the current <code>RM.VALID</code> state.</p> <p>This creates a situation where:</p> <ul> <li>RM history for the pre-case phase is not queryable or auditable.</li> <li>RM transition guards on case-engagement cannot verify that a report was truly   valid before <code>ACCEPTED</code>/<code>DEFERRED</code> was appended.</li> <li>The RM machine's <code>RECEIVE</code> trigger (START \u2192 RECEIVED) is never explicitly   executed anywhere in the <code>vultron.core</code> pipeline.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0013-unify-rm-state-tracking/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Protocol correctness: RM state should be a <li>Simplicity: a single mechanism for RM state is easier to guard and query than   two unconnected mechanisms.</li> <li>Minimal disruption: changes should be incremental and testable.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0013-unify-rm-state-tracking/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ul> <li>Option A \u2014 Persist the full RM lifecycle in When these references use mutable identifiers \u2014 version tags (e.g., <code>@v4</code>) or branch names (e.g., <code>@main</code>) \u2014 a compromised or modified upstream action can silently inject malicious code into CI without any change to the repository. This is a known software supply-chain attack vector.</p> <p>The Vultron project uses GitHub Actions for CI (tests, linting, deployment, link-checking) and needs a sustainable, low-maintenance policy that prevents this class of attack while keeping pins up-to-date.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Prevent supply-chain compromise via tag or branch mutation in upstream   actions.</li> <li>Keep the maintenance burden low so that pins do not become stale.</li> <li>Maintain human-readable context for each pin so that reviewers can   understand which version is pinned without decoding a SHA.</li> </ul>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#considered-options","title":"Considered Options","text":"<ol> <li>SHA-pin every <code>uses:</code> line; use Dependabot for automatic pin updates</li> <li>SHA-pin only third-party (non-<code>actions/</code>) actions</li> <li>Rely on version tags only (no SHA pinning)</li> </ol>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#decision-outcome","title":"Decision Outcome","text":"<p>Chosen option: Option 1 \u2014 SHA-pin every <code>uses:</code> line with Dependabot, because it provides complete protection against tag/branch mutation for all actions (including first-party GitHub actions that are also susceptible), while Dependabot automates the routine maintenance of keeping SHAs current.</p> <p>All six workflow files under <code>.github/workflows/</code> have been updated to pin every <code>uses:</code> reference to a full 40-character commit SHA. Each pin carries an inline comment with the human-readable version tag (e.g., <code># v4.1.0</code>). Dependabot is configured (<code>.github/dependabot.yml</code>) to monitor <code>github-actions</code> on a weekly schedule, providing automatic pull requests whenever a new version is released.</p> <p>An automated pytest test (<code>test/ci/test_workflow_sha_pinning.py</code>) verifies at every CI run that no unpinned <code>uses:</code> line is accidentally introduced.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0014-sha-pin-github-actions/#consequences","title":"Consequences","text":"<ul> <li>Good: Every <code>uses:</code> line is immutable at the referenced commit,   eliminating supply-chain risk from tag or branch mutation.</li> <li>Good: Dependabot opens PRs automatically when new versions are   released, so pins do not become stale without manual tracking.</li> <li>Good: Inline version comments preserve human-readable context for   code review.</li> <li>Good: The automated test (<code>CISEC-01-003</code>) catches any regression   before it reaches <code>main</code>.</li> <li>Neutral: SHA-only references are harder to read without the version   comment, mitigated by the mandatory comment requirement   (<code>CISEC-01-002</code>).</li> <li>Bad: Dependabot may open PRs for patch and minor releases that have   not been security-reviewed; The codebase, however, was built wire-first, so these classes currently live under <code>vultron/wire/as2/vocab/objects/</code> and inherit from the AS2 base class hierarchy (<code>as_Base</code> \u2192 <code>as_Object</code> \u2192 ...).</p> <p>This produces a layer-boundary inversion. The core layer (<code>vultron/core/</code>) is forbidden from importing the wire layer (<code>vultron/wire/as2/</code>); to satisfy that rule, <code>VultronActivity.object_</code> in <code>vultron/core/models/activity.py</code> is typed <code>Any | None</code>. Round-trips through <code>model_dump() \u2192 model_validate()</code> therefore lose typed object identity: nested domain objects deserialize as plain <code>dict</code>s, and <code>DataLayer.hydrate()</code> is silently skipped. PR #577 added an <code>_STUB_OBJECT_MODEL_MAP</code> workaround in <code>outbox_handler.py</code> that covers only <code>VulnerabilityCase</code> and requires per-type manual registration.</p> <p>Wire-format concerns also leak into the domain: AS2 freely models a nested object as an inline object, a bare ID string, or a <code>Link</code> reference, which forces core fields into <code>Object | str | Link | None</code> unions. Behavior-tree code, persistence code, and use-case handlers all pay the cost.</p> <p>Issue #699 tracks the per-type migration. Before any migration can land, core needs a parallel base class hierarchy that mirrors the wire layer's <code>as_Base</code> / <code>as_Object</code> shape \u2014 without inheriting from it. This ADR records the decision to introduce that hierarchy, the naming convention used by the migrated types, and the rule that core fields hold full objects rather than wire-style references. Issue #724 lands only the foundation; no per-type migrations occur in the same change.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0017-domain-wire-object-separation/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>Restore the hexagonal boundary: domain logic lives in <code>core/</code>, wire   logic lives in <code>wire/</code>. Statement","text":"<p>The two-actor demo CI invariant test (<code>test_invariant_5_expected_event_types_present</code>) failed after PR #1024 introduced the CASE_MANAGER role gate on <code>CommitCaseLedgerEntryNode</code>. Investigation (issue #1026) revealed that most vendor-side trigger and received-side use cases never send an activity to the CaseActor's inbox. Consequently the CaseActor's canonical ledger was missing entries for <code>validate_report</code>, <code>ack_report</code>, <code>add_note_to_case</code>, <code>invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, <code>accept_invite_to_embargo_on_case</code>, and <code>close_case</code>.</p> <p>Deeper inspection found that some received-side use cases (<code>note.py</code>, <code>embargo.py</code>) worked around this by resolving the CaseActor's ID from the DataLayer and then executing <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> with <code>actor_id=case_actor_id</code> \u2014 even when the use case was running inside the vendor actor's inbox, not the CaseActor's. This violates the identity contract documented in ADR-0018 and the identity-spoofing pitfall in <code>AGENTS.md</code>: a received-side use case MUST NOT execute a BT with an <code>actor_id</code> different from the actor whose DataLayer is active. The guarded commit BT emits <code>Announce(CaseLedgerEntry)</code> activities as if authored by the CaseActor while running in the wrong actor's outbox context, which is either silently dropped or produces hash-chain divergence.</p> <p>The project has stated this rule in scattered form across <code>AGENTS.md</code>, <code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code>, and <code>specs/case-ledger-processing.yaml</code>, but the explicit, ADR-level statement of the only correct end-to-end path has been missing. As a result, agents and contributors keep re-discovering the shortcut (resolve CaseActor ID, run BT) and believing it is a valid \"delegation\" pattern.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0021-caseactor-inbox-routing-canonical-ledger/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li><code>notes/case-communication-model.md</code> establishes that all post-creation   participant messages route through the Case Actor exclusively.</li> <li>ADR-0018 established a single-writer canonical ledger authored by the   CaseActor. The CaseActor is a participant with extra duties; it is not exempt from CLP-10-001.</p> <p>When the CaseActor originates an activity (e.g., <code>invite_actor_to_case</code>), the activity is addressed to the external recipient(s) via <code>to:</code>. To ensure the CaseActor's own inbox receives the activity for archival, the CaseActor MUST add its own actor ID to the <code>cc:</code> field of the outbound activity. ASGI self-delivery then routes the <code>cc:</code> copy to the CaseActor's received-side use case, where the <code>GuardedCommitCaseLedgerEntryBT</code> fires under the correct <code>actor_id = case_actor_id</code> identity.</p> <p>Why <code>cc:</code> instead of adding <code>case_actor_id</code> to <code>to:</code>: The primary recipient of an <code>Invite(VulnerabilityCase)</code> is the invitee. The CaseActor's copy is an archival side-channel, not a primary delivery. Using <code>to:</code> for both would misrepresent the CaseActor as a co-primary recipient of its own outbound message. <code>cc:</code> preserves the correct semantic: the invitee is in <code>to:</code>, the self-archival copy is in <code>cc:</code>. OX-08-004 narrows its WARNING scope to exclude this purposeful self-copy pattern (the only valid use of <code>cc:</code> in the protocol).</p> <p>The working precedent for this pattern is <code>offer_case_manager_role</code>: its <code>ResolveCaseManagerOfferContextNode</code> sets <code>blackboard.offer_case_manager_to = [case_actor_id]</code> and the Offer is addressed to the CaseActor's own ID in <code>to:</code> (a special case where the CaseActor is genuinely the primary recipient). Delivery for Received-Side CaseActor Routing","text":""},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#context-and-problem-statement","title":"Context and Problem Statement","text":"<p>ADR-0021 established that the CaseActor's own inbox delivery is the sole path to a canonical ledger commit, and introduced a pre-flight guard (CLP-10-002, CLP-10-003): a received-side use case compares <code>receiving_actor_id</code> to the resolved <code>case_actor_id</code> in Python before deciding whether to execute the guarded-commit BT (<code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>).</p> <p>Issue #1036 found that implementing that guard produced a second anti-pattern: every adopting use case now runs two separate <code>BTBridge.execute_with_setup()</code> calls per inbox delivery \u2014 one for the use case's main operation (often under the message's own actor identity, e.g. the invitee or accepting actor), and a second, conditionally dispatched call for the guarded commit (under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>). The condition that decides whether the second call happens at all is plain Python control flow (<code>if receiving_actor_id != case_actor_id: return</code>), not a node inside either tree.</p> <p>An audit (issue #1036, broadened during planning to also resolve a follow-on Concern, issue #1047, which independently named the same anti-pattern in <code>status.py</code> and asked for it to be codified as a spec-level invariant) found the underlying violation in 9 use cases across 6 modules, but not all in the same precise shape. There are three distinct ways the \"execute() does nothing but build one tree, run it once, handle the result\" intent was violated:</p> <p>(1) Genuine actor-identity switching \u2014 a real second <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call under a different actor than the main operation's. This is the literal anti-pattern #1036 and #1047 describe:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/embargo.py</code>:   <code>RemoveEmbargoEventFromCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>InviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code>,   <code>AcceptInviteToEmbargoOnCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree runs under   <code>request.actor_id</code> / <code>invitee_id</code> / <code>accepting_actor_id</code>; a second,   separately constructed <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code>   runs under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. Notably, the main tree (built by   <code>vultron/core/behaviors/embargo/announce_teardown_tree.py</code>'s factory   functions) already composes the identical guarded-commit branch as its   own last child \u2014 but because the main tree executes under the   invitee's/accepting actor's identity, <code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code> inside it   is a guaranteed no-op (that actor is essentially never the CaseActor).   The second, separately-dispatched call is the one that actually fires,   on the rare second attempt under the correct identity. The fix is not   \"add a guarded-commit branch\" (it already exists) \u2014 it is \"stop calling   the tree under the wrong actor a second time, and run the one tree that   already has the branch under <code>receiving_actor_id</code> instead.\"</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/report.py</code>:   <code>ValidateReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main operation is a separate   <code>ValidateCaseUseCase</code> call under <code>actor_id</code>, not even a tree of its own),   <code>AckReportReceivedUseCase</code> (main tree under <code>request.actor_id</code>) \u2014 both   followed by a second, separately-gated guarded-commit call under   <code>receiving_actor_id</code>/<code>case_actor_id</code>.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/status.py</code>:   <code>AddParticipantStatusToParticipantReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 main tree   (<code>add_participant_status_tree</code>) under <code>request.actor_id</code>, then a second   guarded-commit call under <code>case_actor_id</code> via <code>_commit_log_cascade_bt()</code>.   This is the exact site #1047 cited as its primary evidence.</li> </ul> <p>(2) Single BT call, but non-BT procedural code precedes it \u2014 only one <code>execute_with_setup()</code> call exists (the commit), but <code>execute()</code> still does domain-significant work outside any tree before reaching it, so it is not \"build one tree, run it, handle the result\" either:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/note.py</code>: <code>AddNoteToCaseReceivedUseCase</code>   \u2014 appends to <code>case.notes</code>, calls <code>dl.save()</code>, and broadcasts to peers, all   in plain Python, before the single guarded-commit <code>execute_with_setup()</code>   call.</li> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/actor/case_manager_role.py</code>:   <code>OfferCaseManagerRoleReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 idempotent-creates the activity   and calls a trigger-activity port directly in Python, before the single   guarded-commit call. This is a pre-existing BT-06-001 gap (the main   operation was never expressed as a BT at all), not actor-switching.</li> </ul> <p>(3) Single BT call under the correct actor, but assembled ad hoc \u2014 no actor-switching and no procedural code outside the tree, but the tree itself is built inline in <code>execute()</code> rather than via a <code>vultron/core/behaviors/</code> factory function:</p> <ul> <li><code>vultron/core/use_cases/received/case/lifecycle.py</code>:   <code>CloseCaseReceivedUseCase</code> \u2014 constructs a one-off   <code>py_trees.composites.Sequence</code> directly inside <code>execute()</code>, combining   <code>StoreActivityNode</code> and the guarded-commit subtree, and runs it once   under <code>receiving_actor_id</code>. This already satisfies the actor-identity   requirement; the fix here is purely \"move this tree into a named factory   function in <code>behaviors/case/</code>,\" not an actor-switching repair.</li> </ul> <p>All nine sites import <code>create_guarded_commit_case_ledger_entry_tree</code> directly into <code>vultron/core/use_cases/</code>, which is what the structural test (below) detects \u2014 but the underlying defect, and the fix required, differs by category. This is the same class of problem the \"Post-BT Procedural Cascade Anti-Pattern\" (<code>notes/bt-integration.md</code>) already names for the validate\u2192prioritize cascade: a cascade that is a child of the triggering operation in the canonical model must be expressed as a BT subtree, not as a procedural call (or a second, conditionally-dispatched tree execution, or any other domain-significant code) sitting outside the tree in <code>execute()</code>. The fact that the in-tree guard (<code>CheckIsCaseManagerNode</code>) is itself correctly role-gated does not fix category (1): the decision of whether to even ask the question is still made in Python, once per inbox delivery, instead of being one branch of one BT run.</p> <p>A related architectural question raised during planning \u2014 whether the inbox dispatch pipeline itself needs to be restructured so a use case never has to ask \"which actor am I running as\" \u2014 turned out not to apply. Investigation found <code>receiving_actor_id</code> is already resolved before dispatch (<code>FastAPIDispatchAdapter.dispatch()</code>, which sets it from the canonical actor ID resolved off the inbox URL path) and is already present on every received-side event by the time <code>execute()</code> runs. The dispatcher (<code>vultron/core/dispatcher.py</code>) has no CaseActor awareness and needs none \u2014 it is a pure routing-table lookup keyed on <code>semantic_type</code>. The gap is entirely at the use-case/BT boundary, not the dispatch layer; no change to ADR-0020's proposed <code>process_payload</code> seam is required by this decision.</p>"},{"location":"adr/0022-single-bt-execution-for-received-side-case-actor-routing/#decision-drivers","title":"Decision Drivers","text":"<ul> <li>The BT is the domain documentation (<code>specs/behavior-tree-integration.yaml</code>   BT-06-001); a cascade that is invisible outside the tree structure is   invisible to analysis and audit, regardless of whether the gating logic   is \"correct\" in isolation.</li> <li>CLP-09-001 already requires the commit to be reached only through a   role-gated composition \u2014 a Selector/Sequence/Success idiom evaluated   inside the tree.
